speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the order: Government Notices of Motions.
October 22, 1971-The Minister of Transport: That a humble Address be presented to Her Majesty the Queen in the following words:
To the Queen's most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty praying that You may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the Parliament of the United Kingdom to be expressed as follows:
An Act to amend the British North America Act, 1949
Whereas Canada has requested, and consented to, the enactment of the following provisions, and the Senate and House of
Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled have submitted an Address to Her Majesty praying that Her Majesty may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the Parliament of the United Kingdom for that purpose:
Be it therefore enacted by the Queen's most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present Parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows:
Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada amended
1.	Term 17 of the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada set out in the Schedule to the British North America Act, 1949 is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"17. (1) In lieu of section ninety-three of the British North America Act, 1867, the following Term shall apply in respect of the Province of Newfoundland:
In and for the Province of Newfoundland the Legislature shall have exclusive authority to make laws in relation to education, but the Legislature will not have authority to make laws prejudicially affecting any right or privilege with respect to denominational schools, common (amalgamated) schools, or denominational colleges, that any class or classes of persons had by law in Newfoundland at the date of Union, or any like right or privilege with respect to such schools or colleges that any other class or classes of persons have had by law in Newfoundland after the date of Union as members of a religious denomination or one of a group of religious denominations that, by or under the Schools Act of Newfoundland, is or at any time has been recognized as being organized for educational purposes, and out of public funds of the province of Newfoundland provided for education.
(a) all such schools shall receive their share of such funds in accordance with scales determined on a non-discriminatory basis from time to time by the Legislature for all schools then being conducted under authority of the Legislature; and
(b) all such colleges shall receive their share of any grant from time to time voted for all colleges then being conducted under authority of the Legislature, such grant being distributed on a non-discriminatory basis.
(2) In this Term, "Schools Act of Newfoundland" means The Schools Act, 1969, being the Act No. 68 of 1969 (Statutes of Newfoundland), as amended from time to time, or any Act substituted therefor as amended from time to time."
Coming into force of amendment
2.	For greater certainty, the provision of Term of the Terms of Union of Newfoundland with Canada set out in the Schedule to the British North America Act, 1949, in so far as those provisions relate to the aproval and coming into force of the said Terms, do not apply to or in respect of the amendment set out in section 1 of this Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT BANK-APPROVAL OF APPLICATIONS FOR FUNDS
speechtext: The Industrial Development Bank is empowered to make loans to any person engaged or about to engage in an industrial enterprise in Canada (defined as an enterprise in which is carried on any industrial, trade or other business of any kind) provided that it can satisfy itself that credit or other financial resources would not otherwise be available on reasonable terms and conditions, that the amount invested or to be invested in the enterprise by persons other than the Bank and the character of that investment, are such as to afford the IDB reasonable protection and that the enterprise may reasonably be expected to prove successful and able to repay its loan. The statute does not distinguish between enterprises in Canada which are domestically-owned or foreign-owned. The IDB does not maintain records in a form which would provide information concerning either the number or amount of loans to foreign-owned or foreign-controlled businesses in Canada. Notwithstanding the absence of statistical date, the proportion of loans to foreign-owned or foreign-controlled businesses is very small. The IDB's customer's are, primarily, small business enterprises, many of which are proprietorships or partnerships and the average size of loan in fiscal 1971 was about $41,000.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, October 22, consideration in committee of Bill C-259, to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to that act-Mr. Benson-Mr. Honey in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. House again in committee of the whole on Bill C-259, to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to that act. During Friday's sitting, as the Chair understands it, the committee agreed to consider section 109 at this sitting. Shall section 109 carry?
On clause 1-section 109: Deductions permitted by Individuals.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose one could be pardoned for being a little nervous at this stage, but this is now a brand new part of the ball game. When the ball is

October 25, 1971
Income Tax Act
actually handed to you and you start up field with it, you do the best you can. I hope that those words are on the record and that they might get back to the people in the riding of Halifax-East Hants in a newsletter or something.
May I first raise for the consideration of the minister at some time early in our discussion two matters. First of all, may I ask him what we will do if he has kindly second thoughts and decides to bring in further amendments. Second, since our scope is limited when it comes to making proposals to the ministry-we can lead them to water but not necessarily make them drink therefrom- would the minister on occasion be good enough to entertain the thought of adjourning the debate on a particular section so that he can have some discussion with his advisers and perhaps listen to some of the good points that are being made from, no doubt, both sides of the House.
Now I have the preliminaries out of the way, I should like to deal with two specific aspects of what, to most Canadians, is the most important part of the new Income Tax Act. I refer to those magic exemptions that taxpayers claim when they sit down quivering and quaking to make their peace with the Minister of National Revenue, usually as close to April 30 as they can possibly get. If there is anything that the Prime Minister and his party will be able to point to, and for which to thump themselves on the back and stick out their chests, I suspect it will be one of two measures. One is increased exemptions and the other, long delayed, will be the changes brought about in the family allowance structure.
I am sure the government will wax as lyrical as one of its members who described this as just about the ultimate in the way that taxation can wage a successful war against poverty. One then is entitled to ask, as I ask now, whether this does represent a major victory in the war on poverty and whether there is any ammunition being fired, or is the government simply making loud noises with blank cartridges? It is true that compared to the present exemptions the ones proposed by this section are higher, and from that standpoint one can say that the burden on those on lower incomes is reduced. But it is also true-and I think we have to ask ourselves what is a more appropriate figure-that the proposed figures do not even restore those with lower incomes to the position in which they were in 1949. Reflect on that, Mr. Chairman. We can regard 1949 as perhaps the last vintage Liberal year in Canada. There was a high rate of employment. Mr. King had gone off to seek solace in the shadows at Kingsmere and Mr. St. Laurent was in charge. All was well in the best of all possible Canadian worlds.
If one were to translate the happy tranquility of 1949, following the Liberal's return to power with a good number of supporters and the economy in good shape, in terms of today, one would find that the personal exemptions should be at least $1,700 for a single person and $3,400 for a married couple, slightly above the levels we are considering here. There is a further aspect to this. I hope one does not look upon tax reform simply as a matter of trying to adjust from one year to the next in order to take care of any cost of living increase, inflation or suchlike. We have a number of reports which indicate that the poor pay up to 50 per cent of their income in taxes, directly or indirectly, whereas people higher up the

scale earning over $10,000 per year pay roughly a third or about 37 per cent to 38 per cent. In other words, more than half of the dollar a poor man receives goes to some government in some form of taxation. At the more affluent level, only 37 cents of the dollar is paid in taxes.
We have missed the boat in respect of exemptions. We have made some effort to take into account the increased cost of living and inflation, but we have not reached a point of equity. We can consider the rich and the poor and say they are paying 20 per cent, 30 per cent or 40 per cent, whatever it is, and therefore carry their share of the weight, but they do not pay one tittle more. I hope when we attempt to reform our tax system the next time, it will be done by a Conservative administration and, therefore, with some heart. That is one of the things we are after.
A report was received today from the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation at Fort Macleod, Alberta, and I think I should put on the record one of its resolutions. It is:
Resolved, that we petition the federal government to increase the amount of income tax exemption for senior citizens to $3,000 for single people and $4,500 for married couples.
The amount we are to give a single person as a basic exemption, with the additional $650, is $2,150.
When looking at tax reform we should consider exemptions from the point of view of fairness. The rich should pay the same percentage as the poor instead of the poor having to pay a disproportionate amount. The exemptions should also be tied to the cost of living and, perhaps some day, to the poverty level. The figures presented to us do not represent an official poverty level of the Department of National Health and Welfare, or an official level as indicated two or three years ago by the Economic Council of Canada.
A tax credit system might have been a much more equitable way of solving this problem. It would have been more flexible and could take into account those factors to which I have referred. We are faced with a number of anomalies. The Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated in announcing his family income security plan that he feels it costs as much to raise a child of 12 years of age, but the Minister of Finance has indicated that he feels the exemption should be related to age 16. There is a lack of consistency on the part of government in this matter of exemptions, just as there is in respect of the poverty level in Canada. There are many advantages to a tax credit system but in my opening 20 minute statement I cannot go into all the details.
A committee of the House of Commons dealing with this matter noted that while the tax credit approach has a great deal to commend it in terms of being adjustable from time to time without a restructuring of the rate schedule, the exemption procedure does have the advantage of retaining a method to which individual taxpayers are now accustomed. I suppose the best that can be said for that argument is that one is better off with the punches of Cassius Clay, knowing how hard they are, than with the punches of someone else about which you know nothing.
My second point relates to another class of people scattered throughout Canada. This group is not represented and has not presented any petition regarding their tax
October 25, 1971

position. I think their position is worse under the so-called reform bill than it was under the old law. I refer to those involved in common-law marriages. The law does nothing for these people. Let me quote from the Canadian Master Tax Guide, 1970, as prepared by the C C H Canadian Limited, at page 219:
A common-law wife is not considered a spouse and no marital exemption may be claimed on her account. However, if the taxpayer supports a child in a self-contained domestic establishment and the common-law wife acts as a housekeeper, he could claim a $2,000 exemption on account of the child-
An additional deduction can be claimed by reason of the fact that the common-law wife is a full-time servant. Apparently that is her classification. If you think that is puritanical you should consider the plight of the poor lady under this new legislation. For a time I thought she would be covered by clause 109(l)(b) which deals with individuals not entitled to deductions because of an unmarried status, or being married but not supporting or living with a spouse. However, as I read the clause I found that it really did not refer to a common-law spouse but rather is an encouragement to people to live in communes. Apparently you can live in this way and have the advantage of the higher exemption as well as the value of a lady's company. After reading it again I became totally confused, until I finally looked at the three magic words in the marginal note which are "Wholly dependant persons". I knew then we were attempting to do something for the people whose parents are living with them.
I suggest we should have made a step in the direction of helping these people who live in common-law relationships. I see the minister has left and we are to be blessed with his parliamentary secretary and the Liberal whip. I hope they will give some thought to an amendment giving a common-law spouse some protection. I suppose I have just about used my time at this stage, but I felt I should say something in respect of these people who are not represented by any organization. It may sound strange for a Conservative to stand up and argue in favour of those who have not favoured the sanctity of marriage, but we do have an obligation to present their cause when no one else does it for them.
The only hope I see can be found in clause 63 in respect of child care deductions. Perhaps this can be construed in such a way that a woman with a child in a common-law union could in some way charge a baby sitting fee. If a figure could be set, perhaps an exemption would be allowed; but I am not sure the law is that generous. Perhaps a woman in this situation should set up a day nursery in the back yard to look after her own children and other children in the neighbourhood. She might be better off doing this than she is now under the present tax laws. Apart from a very technical approach such as I have taken, I do not think any help is offered these people.
So I do strike a note for these people. I do not know how many there are. I do not know whether there are thousands in society, but sometimes the common law relationship is the easy way out for many people who may not look upon the sanctity of marriage as you, Mr. Chairman, I and others in this Chamber do. I hope something can be done for these people, and that the parliamentary secre-
Income Tax Act
tary will be attentive to the point I make so that another look may be given at this particular matter.
As you probably have gathered, Mr. Chairman, one can range over the gamut in speaking of the particularities of the income tax system and whether the formula we use is correct,-I say it is incorrect-whether all the classes are covered in a comprehensive manner or whether other people should be covered. I know that, as a result of the strictures upon us concerning what we can or cannot do, one is somewhat tied down, but at least one can speak up where there are injustices. I hope the parliamentary secretary will take those I have mentioned into account.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this proposed new section 109 we are now discussing is the one which provides a new level of personal exemptions with regard to income tax. It is the section that would raise the level for single taxpayers from $1,000 to $1,500 and for married taxpayers from $2,000 to $2,850. The section also deals with the matter of exemptions for children, nieces, nephews, aunts, uncles and other dependents. In addition it increases the exemption that is allowed to persons 65 years of age and over from $500 to $650. In that respect it not only provides the increase I have just indicated but provides that this will apply to all persons 65 years and over, whereas this has not been the case since old age security got down to the point where it was paid at age 65. Therefore, this is a pretty important section with which we are dealing. I think it is all the more important when one realizes there have been no changes in the exemption levels since 1949, 22 years ago. As we said repeatedly during the debate on second reading and during the general debate on clause 1, we do not think it is good enough to raise the exemption levels by such small amounts after 22 years in view of what has happened to the cost of living during that period of time.
We feel that at the very least these exemption levels should be $2,000 single and $4,000 married. There are a number of instances in which the exemption levels might even be higher. However, before I get into a plea to raise the exemption levels, I wish we could engage either the minister or the parliamentary secretary in a discussion about tax credits rather than exemption levels, as a way of dealing with this matter. The hon. member for Halifax-East Hants made reference to this in the remarks he just made. The other day the hon. member for Cardigan proposed a rather ingenious device, which if I may say so struck me as comparable to the concept of tax credits. I do not think I am being unfair to the hon. member for Cardigan when I say he feels these fixed exemption levels, arbitrary as they are, do not take into account the cost of living needs of the people in the lower bracket, people with large families, older people and so on. As I say, rather than our having a long list of set speeches, in view of the fact that we are in committee of the whole where we can speak as often as we want and have back and forth discussions, I wish the parliamentary secretary, since he is here on behalf of the minister at this time, would get into this discussion.
I know this matter has been discussed at length before the standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I know that the committee considered all the arguments and that the majority report of that committee

October 25, 1971
Income Tax Act
came down for exemption levels rather than a system of tax credits. Surely, however, it is clear that any system of tax exemptions tends to give the greater benefit to those in the upper and higher brackets. Any system of tax exemptions makes it impossible to meet the kind of special need the hon. member for Cardigan spoke about the other day. One can see this in the effect of the figures that are before us at the present time. I have before me a table that has been worked out showing what the adjusted rates do to people of various income levels. A single person whose gross income was $2,000 when the exemption level was $1,000 had to pay a tax of $109. When the exemption level becomes $1,500 he will pay only $75. This is fine. It is a reduction, but it is a reduction of only $34. On the other hand, a single person with an income of $25,000 under the $1,000 exemption paid $8,945 whereas with the $1,500 exemption level he will pay only $8,468 which is a saving of $297.
I submit that is a very good example of what the exemption level method of dealing with this matter does. It provides a few dollars to those in the lower brackets and provides ever so much more for those in the upper brackets. The table I have in front of me gives the figures for various other income levels, but I need not put them all on the record. The higher the income the more one saves under the exemption method level. On the other hand, by a tax credit system it is possible, as Carter shows, to treat all income from the first dollar as taxable, and to then set a figure such that persons below that figure get a credit that offsets the tax charged against them and therefore pay no tax at all. If ,in order to bring this thing to a head later on we have to move an amendment to raise the exemption levels to $2,000 and $4,000,1 am prepared to do so. I can see procedural troubles, but we will worry about them when they arise. But I would rather not move that kind of amendment because it would only exaggerate the very thing about which I am complaining.
Therefore, I wish that instead we could persuade the government to accept a system of tax credits. The government argued before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and that committee contended in its report that you can achieve the same thing if at the time you raise your exemption levels you adjust the rates. It does not work out that way. The figures that I have given show that it is just about impossible to adjust the rates in a manner that will not be of tremendous benefit to those at the top. But if we can get started with a tax credit system, we could then provide that single persons below a $2,000 income and married persons below a $4,000 income pay no tax regardless of what the calculations might charge against them.
In the same way, this could be applied with respect to children, especially children who make up a large family. You cannot really be fair under this exemption system because the wealthy get more exemptions when they have more children, although I have been told that the wealthy do not have more children. At any rate, they do get quite a bit more in this way and the poorer families that may have more children get precious little out of the exemption system. The same thing applies to the extra exemption for person 65 years of age and over. I welcome the

fact that the level has been raised to $650. As a matter of fact, I still think the government should make it retroactive to January 1, 1971, and I welcome the fact that it will now apply to all persons 65 years of age or over whether or not they are drawing old age security. But here again, you introduce the same element of unfairness because the very wealthy person who gets old age security at the age of 65 will receive an additional $960 a year, $650 of that being non taxable, which is quite a bonanza to that person but it is not much of a bonanza to older people on lower incomes.
Again, this could be taken care of quite easily by having a system of tax credits as I suggested, one system of tax credits for single persons and families who are of working age, a system of tax credits for children, and a special system of tax credits for older people. I agree with the plea that has been made by the pensioners organization as reported a moment ago by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants. I put on the record myself that $3,000 for a single person and $4,500 for a married couple is a reasonable figure for senior citizens, but you do not need that for the very wealthy person. What you need is to guarantee that no older person who has an income of $3,000 a year will have any of that taken away in tax. Go ahead and tax the wealthy, whether they are 65, 70 or 75. There are not many up there but there are some. But with respect to those who really need some consideration, the best way to give it is by a system of tax credits.
I have already said, but perhaps I might repeat it, that we would have to have different sets of credits for different categories-one credit for single and married working people, another credit for children, and a special credit for people of a certain age. I suggest that this is a way that would be much more fair than the exemption level system. I know that one of the replies from the government side of the House is that people do not understand the tax credit system, that people like the idea of knowing that there is $1,000 or $2,000 or whatever you have that is tax free, but they would very soon understand it once the system came into effect.
So, Mr. Chairman, I welcome the contribution made in this area the other day by the hon. member for Cardigan and I welcome the contribution made just now by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants. Now, I should like to hear from the government side on this issue. Later on if we get nowhere, I am prepared to move that the exemption levels be raised to $2,000 and $4,000, but if we do that without adjusting the rates we will provide more for those in the upper income brackets. I hope that fairly soon we will hear from the government side with respect to the whole question of tax credits which I think is a better way of establishing equity in a tax system than the exemption level system that is being perpetuated in this bill.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege. I think it is a matter which I have to bring to the attention of this House as soon as I can. I will raise it again tomorrow probably when Mr. Speaker is in the Chair. There is a Canadian Press story in today's Citizen which is headed "Tax Bill Delays Close of Session". Included in the story is this sentence:
Informants said the government has offered the opposition a week or two extra Christmas holidays if there is a fast completion of the tax legislation.
October 25, 1971
Shame.
The reporter must have been smoking government marijuana.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Government members appear to be on a perpetual holiday. However, I will not deal with that. But I want to say that this is an unmitigated lie if it is, in fact, a statement made by an informant in the government. I am sure my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will bear me out when I say that at the various House leaders' meetings which we have had with regard to this matter, the House leaders were interested in working out an orderly way of dealing with this bill. As usual, the government got itself in a mess in its legislative program, and we came up with a series of proposals which would permit us to contest the repugnant parts of the bill and deal with the others in due course. It was a suggestion for the orderly treatment of the bill which formed the basis of discussion. This is the kind of thing which makes it exceedingly difficult to work out programs. We offer our help to get the government out of the mess and then we are faced with a situation of this kind. I am raising the matter now because it is the first opportunity. I may have an opportunity to raise it again with Mr. Speaker in the chair tomorrow.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I take it the hon. member for Peace River, as he indicated, was giving advance notice of a question of privilege he may or may not wish to raise when His Honour is in the chair. Of course, that is recorded.

Mr. Chairman, I listened very attentively to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, whose diligence and sincerity everyone in this Parliament appreciates, but one wonders whether, in his keen desire to help, he does not get mixed up and is unable to tell us from what source that help will come. From the remarks to which I listened I gathered that, first, he was criticising the government for not bringing in a system of tax credits, particularly for those Canadians in the lower income brackets. Through you, Mr. Chairman, may I respectfully point out to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the reason for the omission of the tax credit system is obvious. A large number of the members of this House sat for many months, not just two or three months, studying the white paper and the tax bill presented by the government, then brought in a recommendation that tax credits were not appropriate to our Canadian tax system. The Committee recommended that, instead of using tax credits, we should use tax exemptions, which is what the government has done in this bill.
Really, Mr. Chairman, I think that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should be a bit more fair. He should tell the people of Canada that the reason the government is not bringing in tax credits is that specialists in the field, who have examined this question very closely, have recommended that tax credits not be used but that tax exemptions be used instead.

Do you only do what your specialists tell you to do?
Income Tax Act

In fact, in this particular instance, the government has done what the specialists of the Conservative party recommended, because every one of them recommended that there be tax exemptions and not tax credits. So I say to the hon. member, next time don't put your foot in your mouth quite so far.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said he would introduce some sort of amendment to raise the tax exemptions to $2,000 for single people and $4,000 for married couples. As you know, Mr. Chairman, the existing exemption for a single person is $1,000. I do not always agree with the government, but in this instance I believe that the government quite rightly proposes that the exemption be raised from $1,000 to $1,500. If the hon. member were fair, he would tell the people of Canada that this change is going to cost the Minister of National Revenue exactly $500 million in tax revenues, because every $100 of exemption costs the government $100 million. This exemption, within a matter of a few dollars, will cost half a billion dollars.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre could quite rightly ask the government, "Where are you going to get this half billion dollars"? A responsible government has a duty to reply, and I assume the Minister of Finance or his parliamentary secretary would say, "We are going to get the money by initiating a capital gains tax in Canada." I point out that a capital gains tax has been recommended by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and by many other people, including the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs which considered this matter for many months. But what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre does not tell us is where the money would be obtained to make up the loss in revenue if his recommendation were implemented to increase the exemption for single people from $1,500 to $2,000. Mr. Chairman, you do not have to take my word for this. You do not have to take the word of any member of this House. Just look up the facts and figures that can be obtained from any library in Canada and you will find that raising the exemption from $1,500 to $2,000 will cost a further half billion dollars.
That isn't correct.
That is absolutely true. Are you doubting my word?
I think your figure is too high.
Are you doubting my word? I understand that in this House you either put up or shut up.
Oh, come off it.
Don't you open that mouth of yours, George. I shut it one night, you may remember.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please.
I don't mind professionals, Mr. Chairman, but these amateurs!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I think the discussion is very interesting, but I make a plea to all hon. members to direct their contributions to the Chair.

October 25, 1971
Income Tax Act

In any event, from the figures I have read, increasing the exemption from $1,500 to $2,000 for single people, and from $2,000 to $4,000 for married couples, will cost in the general area of half a billion dollars, and I believe that that figure is too low, if anything. We all know how sincere is the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. As I told him the other day, if he had happened to live at the same time as our Lord was on earth there would have been 13 disciples instead of 12, because he wants to give things away. If he is absolutely sincere, then he will tell this House where he would get the extra half billion dollars.
Hear, hear!

Of course, he does say, "We will tax the rich." If he carries his sincerity as far as I hope he does, then he will tell us how many rich people there are in Canada. I tell you, Mr. Chairman, there are very few rich persons in Canada. Every year several hundred of them are leaving Canada because they are being taxed too much now. If you don't believe me ask some of our honourable friends from Alberta, and they will explain the situation to those who do not understand. When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggests that a single person making $25,000 a year will get more through a tax exemption than he will through a tax credit, again if he is fair he will tell us how many single people there are in Canada making $25,000 a year. I would say there are very few indeed. So, so far as the exemption situation is concerned, I think the government has brought forward a very fair bill.
I suggest that the government, in proposing an exemption of $650 for those who are 65, can be very proud because we know that no country in the world has given such exemptions to people of that age. We are giving higher exemptions to, and taking less taxes from, people at age 65 who are getting the old age pension, than any other country in the world.
Hear, hear!

Of course, we would like to be able to establish higher exemptions, perhaps up to $10,000. Why stop at $2,000 for single people and $4,000 for married people? The fact is that somebody has to pay taxes to provide the benefits that we enjoy. Therefore, without prolonging my remarks further, I simply say that while all of us wish the exemption could be more than $1,500, we must consider the facts in this day and age when more benefits are coming from governments, whether federal or provincial, when governments are producing more costly programs, such as medicare, hospital services, higher old age pensions and higher children's allowances. Taking all this into account, I would say an exemption of $1,500 is a good start and will benefit many people in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Bruce who just spoke made some very interesting comments on the tax bill and the amount of revenue that the exemptions are going to cost the federal treasury. However, I think it is difficult to enter into this type of calculation without reference to the fiscal dividends which accrue to
[The Deputy Chairman.]
governments as a result of inflation. A number of hon. members were members of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs which studied the bill. It became evident at these hearings that it was possible to reduce the tax rate and still increase the total revenue of the government as a result of inflation. I say that is possibly what is happening at the present time.
If there are any attractive features in this 707-page bill, they lie in the fields of personal income tax and personal exemptions. I think we can safely say that the increase in personal exemptions and the increased limits on contributions to pension plans do little more than reflect the erosion in the value of the dollar over the years. The last time the tax exemptions were raised was in 1949, so this change is long overdue. The reduction in the top combined rates to 61.1 per cent affects few people. Perhaps it is unrealistic to accept the stated rates when several provinces already levy taxes at rates above the standard 30 per cent used in arriving at the combined level of provincial and federal rates referred to in the tax summary.
To return to the matter of the fiscal dividends, we know that in past years Canada's rate of inflation has been as high as 6 per cent and rarely lower than 3 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. parliamentary secretary rises on a point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it was my understanding that the arrangements made between party leaders, and announced in the House by the President of the Privy Council on Friday, were to the effect that remarks would be strictly relevant to the proposed sections of the act under consideration, sections 109 and 110. The general economy, trends in inflation, and rates schedules are not mentioned, so I was wondering when the hon. member was going to relate his remarks to the particular section under consideration.
They are all tied in.

Mr. Chairman, that is a very interesting comment made by the parliamentary secretary. Was he not sitting here a few minutes ago when the hon. member for Bruce made his remarks? Why was he not on his feet then? He was too busy applauding, but the relevance of those remarks was very difficult to understand indeed.
It will take that much longer, Pat. Just be quiet.
If I may refer to the matter of fiscal dividends that accrue to governments by allowing the inflation rate to continue-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. With all respect to the hon. member for Battle River, I did wonder if he was not going a bit beyond section 109 which is presently before the committee. If I am in error I know he will point out where I err, but I think we are essentially dealing, as the heading indicates, with the computation of taxable income. The section sets out the various exemptions of people who qualify and so on. I would invite the hon. member to confine his remarks within the four corners of section 109.
October 25, 1971

With the greatest respect, Mr, Chairman, may I point out that when we are discussing personal income, certain exemptions are set out and the balance of income is subject to tax on the basis of rates. If the hon. member wishes to comment on the adequacy or inadequacy of the exemption, surely he is within his rights to refer perhaps to the attitude of the government in wanting to continue, as it does, the system of a general flat rate. The flat exemption results in an inflationary bonus for the government; it is as simple as that and surely reference can be made to it. I agree that we are somewhat more limited but not as strictly as suggested by the parliamentary secretary. If we are to proceed in this way, it will be a long haul to complete the discussion of these sections.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps there is a disposition on the part of members of the opposition, since they cannot deal with exemptions without dealing with rates, to extend the purview of the current debate to include section 117 which does cover rates. Perhaps we cannot deal with one without the other. Is that the disposition?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I want to be as helpful as possible, and certainly do not want to restrict hon. members. I agree in essence with the hon. member for Edmonton West, although it is a matter of degree. I think the hon. member will recognize that, although his remarks may be relative, they might be considered to be a bit outside the four corners of the section; they must be relevant. The hon. member for Battle River.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I am happy that you bore with me through the preamble. As the hon. member for Edmonton West pointed out, there is a very close association between the rates and the personal income tax section of the bill.
I wanted to comment on the surtax which has been repealed. I do not think anyone can quarrel with that, but when we look at it we see that the surtax was really not a tax on income but a tax on a tax. This affects income retention for only a very few people who were, in practical terms, paying a maximum of 11 per cent. Very few Canadian Taxpayers will find their income increased as a result of this change because the tax amounted to only about one-third of one per cent or about $3 for every $1,000 of earned income. Bearing in mind the present rate of inflation, if individuals do not have an increase in earnings in the next three weeks, they will be back where they started before the surtax was removed. This is quite an accurate calculation of what this means to the economy in terms of real dollars.
Elasticity is a word which becomes familiar when we speak of the tax structure and personal income tax rates. I suggest that the new tax rates have been geared to an even greater extent to the concept of progressive income tax rates. This results in an increase and not a decrease in the tax payable.
Let me take an example from the lower income brackets. A single person earning $1,700 a year would, under the present tax system, claim exemptions of $1,100 and pay $70 tax on his taxable income of $600. If his income rises to $1,800, his taxable income is $700 and he pays $81 in tax. Thus, although his income has risen by 6 per cent,
Income Tax Act
his tax has increased by 17 per cent. It will be seen that under the new tax legislation, every 10 per cent increase in income in similar circumstances is accompanied by an 18 per cent increase in taxes. The tax increase under the new bill represents a higher ratio with respect to the proportion of take-home pay than was the case under the old legislation.
I do not wish to go much further at this point than merely point out these anomalies in connection with tax rates. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent, in directing a question during the question period to the Minister of Agriculture, referred to the fact that a poultry quarantine station had been set up in the middle of the poultry district of southern Ontario. It seems to me that the type of mentality that was responsible for that has manifested itself in the ministry that is responsible for taxation.

Mr. Chairman, my intervention will be brief and, I hope, specific in form. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who argues, and has argued for years, that exemptions are too low and that we are taxing people at the poverty level. He says that by so doing we compound the problem of poverty, something that Economic Council reports have pointed out over and over again. As I say, we compound the problem of poverty by adding an additional burden of tax on those who are poor. We realize that the government has difficulty in raising money. Nevertheless, we on this side of the House have suggested how the government might accomplish its aim of greater revenues for the treasury which are necessary in order to provide those benefits which we feel must be provided for an enlightened and progressive country.
The hon. member for Bruce is an interesting and able speaker and likes to keep an argument going. He asked pointedly from what source the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre thinks all this extra money will come. Instead of answering, may I ask this: From what source did the $1 billion that the Minister of Finance is to make available in connection with winter works, and so on, come? His program calls for $1 billion in benefits. Without going into any great preamble, may I say that we know the source of this money which is to be used for winter works relief. It will come from the people who are paying taxes now; that is where the money will come from, even though the government may borrow the money in the beginning. You see, with taxes being paid on incomes of $5,000 a year and even less, there is little difference between the working poor who are taxed and welfare recipients who receive those taxes. So, by depriving one group of society we are encouraging those who receive low incomes and those who receive welfare to argue about their respective situations, because both groups are in deprived circumstances. I had not intended speaking on this point and have raised it only by way of preamble.
I had intended referring to an anomaly in the former tax law which encouraged the administrators of the act, so to speak, to take a moral position. My remarks will be in a similar vein to those that were made a few moments ago by the hon. member for Halifax East-Hants. Perhaps I could most efficiently deal with my concern by reading a series of letters exchanged between the Minister of Finance and myself. They concern the fact that a person

October 25, 1971
Income Tax Act
who has been ordered by the court to support an illegitimate child not domiciled with him received no recognition under the previous act of the amount spent. This matter may or may not have been corrected in the new legislation. I am referring to subsection (5) of section 109, the "partial dependency" subsection.
May I be permitted to quote from a series of three letters, the first one being dated December 3, 1968. I should say, before I begin, that I am not speaking in favour of illegitimacy. I feel that the law itself should take a neutral position on this matter. At the moment it does not. May I quote from my letter to the Minister of Finance of December 3, 1968? It reads in part:
This concerns the payment of support and maintenance of a child not domiciled under the same roof as the person who is required to supply this support and maintenance. My constituent has written me stating that these payments have been disallowed as a deduction for income tax purposes.
I would appreciate it if you would tell me if the Income Tax Act has been fairly imposed in this case. If the Income Tax Act makes no provision for such a deduction it appears to me that some amendment should be considered so that anomalies such as this might be overcome. Certainly the man who is required to pay this type of support and is doing so is fulfilling the obligations the Court placed upon him and does not have the use of this money for his own living expenses. It seems unfair to me that anyone should be additionally punished by the failure of the Income Tax Act to recognize the partial dependency of the child in question.
I asked the minister to write and provide me with some information. Actually, my letter was preceded by a letter dated September 8 which the minister wrote to my constituent. The second paragraph reads:
Under the present laws, a taxpayer may deduct from his income for the year only those amounts expended for a child who, during that year, was wholly dependent upon him for support. A request such as yours would require an amendment to the Income Tax Act-
I might add that the preceding paragraph related to deductions for tax purposes with respect to payments made by the putative father of an illegitimate child.
Following the letter I wrote and the information I received, I again wrote to the Minister of Finance. My letter said in part that the minister had directed me to look at a certain section of the act, and I suggested that we ought to delete the phrase "of the marriage" where it appears twice in the section, since this wording seems to work against the particular individual concerned. I went on to say in the letter I wrote to the Minister of Finance, dated January 20, 1969, as follows:
This, then, would place my constituent in a position equivalent to married couples not living together who are making payments for child maintenance, or payments required by the court under conditions of separation and divorce.
My constituent . . . has been ordered by the court to pay out for the maintenance of an illegitimate child the sum of $3,840 over a period of 16 years. Because of present tax regulations and rates, he is additionally assessed $1,099.20 for his indiscretion. This seems markedly punitive to me and I would be pleased if you would consider this regulation during the current tax review.
We are now considering the tax review legislation in committee of the whole. I think the argument is quite clear. In this instance, the drafters of the law are taking a moral stand. The person who is required to pay for the support is really, except in the legal and spiritual obligations of marriage, in the same position as any other parent supporting or partially supporting a child. He is entitled to

deduct this amount. I do not see any reason, in the light of the situation of the constituent I have just described, why this deduction privilege should not also apply in the case of an illegitimate child or a court order payment for support of an illegitimate child. There may be thousands of cases like this across Canada.
I am not suggesting that the court has no right to make an order for support. If the support is given, the money is not for the use of the father or mother, depending on which way it works. I would appreciate it if the experts of the tax department and the parliamentary secretary would consider this matter carefully. It may not be a great thing, but the fact that the tax law should be blind as far as this moral or ethical question is concerned, is a valid point. Because they are reasonable men, I hope they will look into this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am delighted to have the opportunity to accept the invitation extended earlier from across the way to comment at least on some of the points raised. Perhaps I should deal first with the point raised by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West.
The proposed section 109(5) of the new act is very much the same as section 26(6) of the present act. It is quite possible that the parent of an illegitimate child who does not have direct care or custody of that child could qualify for all or part of the exemption that is attributable to that child, depending on establishing the relative degree of support which he affords it. I think on reflection the hon. member will agree that the amount of money which a parent pays for the care and support of his own child in his own household, one who is acknowledged and legitimate, is not available to spend for other purposes. That parent is in precisely the same position as the parent of an illegitimate child.
As I understand the hon. member's argument, he thinks that moneys paid under a court order in this situation should be a form of deduction in taxable income. I suppose if one afforded that privilege to the parent of an illegitimate child, one could not discriminate or make a moral judgment by denying it to the parent of a legitimate child. It would be a very worth-while tax avoidance ploy for parents to get maintenance orders from judges so that they could deduct the amounts paid under those maintenance orders rather than accept the exemption granted under the act. The parent of an illegitimate child in the present circumstances is entitled to claim an exemption or partial exemption, depending on the extent to which he is supporting the child. I refer the hon. member to section 109(5).
I now wish to deal with the main thrust of the arguments raised by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre regarding the adequacy in the increase in exemptions. We must acknowledge that if the $1,000 exemption was adequate in 1949, then certainly it is not adequate in 1971 and will not be adequate in 1972. However, the arithmetic application of the cost of living index to those exemptions is an oversimplification. It fails to take into account many social programs such as medicare, hospitalization and family allowances which have been established and/or
October 25, 1971

improved over the years. They have relieved all Canadians, including low income Canadians, of some of the demands on their personal resources that existed in 1949.
Frankly, I do not think the simple application of the cost of living index is a persuasive argument to support any specific exemption that you may decide upon. We have higher exemptions. This will remove about one million Canadians from the tax rolls and reduce taxes for five million others. While I am sure nothing would make the government happier than to be able to offer the tax paying public even more generous exemptions than those contained in Bill C-259, these were settled upon after a great deal of thought had been given to all the implications, both from the point of view of revenue as well as the taxpayers. They are certainly not inadequate exemptions.
The tax credit system is certainly something that has some merit. However, if there is a country in the world that has tried it and has made it work, I am not aware of it. Certainly, the exemption and graduated rate system that the government has opted for in Bill C-259 is not nearly as inflexible as the more outspoken advocates of the tax credit system indicate. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was most honest when he indicated, at the close of his remarks, that a tax credit system would probably have to involve a different tax credit depending on whether you were married, had children and how many children you had. If the tax credit system were to be fair, it would not be nearly as simple and straight forward as many of its advocates would have us believe.
It is the same thing as a flat rate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The fundamental fact is that there is no magic in it. Revenue conceded to low income Canadians by increasing tax credits would have to be made up some place else. This is a very simple fact. You do not avoid it by accepting a system of tax credits.
Take it from the oil industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The progressive tax system we have in Canada does, of course, levy a much heavier tax on higher income Canadians than lower. Higher income Canadians have come to expect to pay taxes to take care of this fact. However, the increase in exemptions, combined with the progressive rate of tax, does, in the view of the government, achieve the objects that we desire.
I refer hon. members to the schedule for single status taxpayers in Canada as compared to other countries of the world. Under the new bill, single status taxpayers, assuming that they are employed in business, will pay taxes when their income reaches $1,650. That compares to $1,773 in the United States, $1,011 in the United Kingdom and $470 in Australia. The married situation in Canada is such that married taxpayers will pay taxes after their income has reached $3,041. This compares to $2,533 in the United States, $1,445 in the United Kingdom and $470 in Australia. I do not think we have to apologize to anyone for the net effect and benefits that the increased exemption schedule proposed in Bill C-259 affords to our lower income tax payers.

taxed, which would mean that the government could easily raise basic exemptions or institute the system of tax credits that we have been proposing.
I know the parliamentary secretary comes from Calgary, which is the headquarters of the oil industry in the province, and that he has a special interest in protecting the oil industry. However, let me put on the record a few more figures. The parliamentary secretary, in one of his usual, stupid interjections, asked me whether I had the permission of the Premier of Manitoba to say the things I was saying. Let me summarize for the edification of the parliamentary secretary-if that is possible-a statement made by the Minister of Finance of the province of Manitoba on July 16, 1971.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The gospel according to St. Paul.

I would sooner take the gospel according to St. Paul than the gospel according to St. Pat. The Minister of Finance of the province of Manitoba, commenting on these proposals that we are discussing today, suggested that we replace the tax exemptions that this government is putting forward with a system of tax credits. He suggested that all income, regardless how it is earned, be included as income for purposes of taxation. That cannot be a very radical proposal since it is precisely the proposal that was made by the Carter commission, which was headed by a man appointed by a Conservative government. He suggested that the natural resources industry be taxed on the same basis as other industry.
He then went on to spell out in detail what these changes would mean in terms of dollars. Even using the then tax structure, raising personal exemption to $1,500 from $1,000, as proposed by the government, would mean nothing to people who have no income. This is precisely why we are proposing tax credits, because it is these people who need assistance but who will not get one red cent from the proposal made by this government.
The Minister of Finance of the province of Manitoba also pointed out that for those people whose income matches the exemption level, the new increase to $1,500 will mean a saving of $250, or $463 for those with an income of $10,000, or $1,236 for those people with an income in excess of $400,000 a year. So that those who have will get, as is usual with this government. The proposed exemption of $2,850 for a married couple will result in no saving to those with an income of less than $2,850. It will mean a saving of $551 for those with an income of $250 and who are now receiving an exemption of $2,000. It will mean a saving of $845 for people with an income of $10,000, or $2,348 for people with an income in excess of $400,000. As I said before, those who have will get more.
From the revenue point of view, the Minister of Finance of Manitoba pointed out that, if a system of tax credits were adopted rather than the system of exemptions, an additional $1,140 million would be brought in because the

government would begin to tax people on everything they have and be able to give relief to those people who need it the most. Using tax credits in place of exemptions would bring in $250 million. Full inclusion of capital gains in income rather than the proposed system of half rates on capital gains would bring in another $100 million. The elimination of dividend tax credits would bring in another $139 million, and the elimination of depletion allowances for natural resource industries and the three-year exemption with no offsetting provision, which the government is continuing, would together account for another $224 million. If you limited the capital cost allowances to actual wear and tear, as the hon. member for Duvernay proposed in his speech to the Canadian Economics Association, you would bring in another $360 million. We must add to that the $65 million which would be brought in as a result of the retention of the estate and gift tax legislation which this government is so easily giving up. All in all, the proposals which the Minister of Finance of Manitoba made would bring in not the $500 million odd, which the hon. member for Bruce is worrying about, but $3,282 million. It is obvious that the money is available if you want to find it. If you want to tax those who have money instead of those who have not, as we have done so frequently in the past, this amount of money can be raised.
Let me say a few words about the question of a tax credit system as compared to the tax exemption system. The hon. member for Bruce said the committee which dealt with the question listened to all the experts who all came out for a system of tax exemption rather than a tax credit system. If that is true the committee must have looked carefully for the experts they wanted, those who would give them the kind of answers that suited the government. These people must be doing very well as a result of our inadequate and inequitable tax system. The most thorough and fair study of our tax system was carried out by the Carter Commission. It recommended that we institute a system of tax credits. We also propose that the present tax exemption system should be eliminated and replaced by a system of tax credits.
A tax credit and exemption system are both intended to recognize that a certain amount of an individual's income must be free of tax. We are appalled by the fact that a large number of people who, according to the Economic Council of Canada, are living in a state of poverty will be paying income tax, even after we increase the basic exemptions as proposed by this government to $1,500 for a single person and $2,850 for a married couple. The members of the Economic Council of Canada, appointed by the present government, are not noted as being wildeyed radicals. According to their calculations in respect of the status of poverty, a large number of people will still be paying income tax.
The present legislation specifically states that the exemption will be $1,500 for a single person. The tax credit system does not state the amount of income which should be exempt, but does state the amount of tax that should not be paid in the form of a deduction. The tax credit comes off in the form of a tax credit equivalent to the monthly tax payment. The tax exemption system provides a greater amount of tax benefit to the upper income
October 25, 1971

tax payers than the lower income tax payers. I have already indicated examples of that, and how the tax exemptions proposed by the government will give a greater advantage to the higher income group than to the group at the bottom of the taxable income level. It is for that reason we have proposed a system of tax credits rather than a tax exemption system.
The parliament secretary suggests that the matter is not as simple as we have suggested. No tax system is simple. He suggested a tax credit system would have to be varied for different groups, depending on whether the people are single or married. Certainly the parliamentary secretary knows, if he knows anything at all, that the tax exemptions system does precisely that. It says a person who is single will not pay, according to the present proposal, on his first $1,500 of income, and that a married couple will not pay on the first $2,850 of income. A family of three or more will have a further exemption. In that respect, the tax credit system we propose is in no different from the tax exemption system.
What we have said, and will continue to say, is that the present system of taxation and the present exemption levels as proposed by the government are not equitable. They place an undue burden on those with lower incomes. For the benefit of the hon. member for Bruce who said, among other very interesting things, there are fewer millionaires and wealthy people than there used to be because we are taxing them so heavily, let me refer to an article which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of April 21, 1969. It is written by Mr. D. H. Fullerton who is well-known to members of this House. He has held a number of positions with the federal government and is an economist and an expert on taxation. After pointing out that a survey in the United States indicated there were 21 people there with incomes of over $1 million per year who paid no taxes at all, Mr. Fullerton went on to state:
Precisely similar data for Canada is not available, but experts in the field agree that the Canadian rich have been just as successful as their American counterparts in finding ways to cut their tax bill. One of the wealthiest men in Canada, in fact, is known to pay no income tax at all. The Canadian tax avoidance methods, however, tend to differ a bit from the American.
The fact that they differ will not be of much comfort to those taxpayers at the bottom end of the taxable scale who know that these people are avoiding taxes. Mr. Fullerton went on to state:
Wealthy Canadians do not have the same benefits on oil depletion but are adept at using others. The favourite Canadian devices appear to be cost chargeable to real estate operations, and various methods for converting current income into tax-free or almost tax-free capital gains, such as setting up a holding company in West Indian tax havens.
Put this on the record because I want my friends on the other side not to feel so sorry for those who have done very well in this country. Mr. Fullerton, in this article, makes a very clear distinction between tax evasion, which is illegal, and tax avoidance, which is quite proper and legal as long as we are stupid enough not to plug the holes.
But very immoral.

My colleague says it is immoral, but one cannot blame these people for trying to live within the limits of the law. One cannot blame them for hiring qualified tax lawyers who specialize in tax matters in order to
Income Tax Act
get the advice they need. One might wish that the ordinary citizen could afford the same kind of highly technical advice which is available to the wealthy of this country.
As Mr. Fullerton said so clearly, the fact is that the wealthy in this country have done well up until now and they will continue to do well when we give effect to the tax bill the government proposes. Those in the lower income brackets in this country who do not earn enough to pay any income tax, as is the case in respect of so many farmers and so many people in the maritime provinces, will receive no benefit from these proposed changes. Those in the lower income brackets who have a taxable income will continue, as they have for so many years with the approval of the parliamentary secretary obviously, to pay a much higher percentage of their income in the form of taxes-income taxes, sales taxes and real estate taxes- than those in the upper brackets who will continue to get off very lightly as they have for so many years.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry if I sound a little like a Canada goose this afternoon, but the cold I picked up last week has not gone away. The minister of health and I must have the same physician because what has been prescribed for us has not been very successful. In any event, I shall do my best to get through this. At the outset may I say the way in which we are dealing with these sections is somewhat of an experiment as a result of consultations between the government House leader, myself and others, concerning how this bill should be handled. It is purely an experiment in some ways and I would hope, in dealing with the general sections on personal income, and having considered shall we say these two sections which group themselves very nicely, that perhaps when the time comes-I do not know when it will be because it depends entirely on the House- we would go to those sections, for instance sections 3 to 8, which involve the computation of income. We are now looking at certain deductions. There are further deductions more minor in nature which lead us further astray in section 111.
Having outlined the plan, I may say that sections 117 and 118 involve the rates, but this is an incidental reference. If we look at this bill we will note that some of the sections and subsections on pages 277 and 289 are merely carrying forward the provisions of the old act. There is some modification in certain areas, changes of a few words, which we hope will be an improvement. There is no guarantee about this and, as a matter of fact, there are some commentaries which suggest these changes are merely more confusing. Then, there are new principles of taxation. Therefore, I believe we must look at what is new. Some portions of the bill which merely carry forward provisions that have been in existence for many years may prove to be wrong. I believe the hon. member for Fraser Valley had something to say about that and I believe we will have something to say about other sections. Certainly, mention must be made of the relationship between husband and wife and the income the wife may earn from a firm in which her husband may be a partner.
The basic thrust I want to make is that which I made back at the time of the committee hearings on the white

October 25, 1971
Income Tax Act
paper in respect of personal exemptions. Notwithstanding what was said by the hon. member for Bruce, I was not one whit impressed by the arguments of those who insisted that this is a better system than the tax credit system. For one thing, the amount of exemption applies to every category of taxpayer. Be he low income, middle income or the highest income individual in the country, he will still come under this provision of $1,500 per taxpayer. This is a tax system which is predicated upon the principle of ability to pay. The total tax system of this country provides no recognition of the fact that the low income taxpayer pays an equal shot with the high income tax payer under customs, sales tax and the many other types of tax in this country. So, it seems to me that for this reason it would be easier to differentiate between the categories of taxpayers in the broad sense by using a tax credit system, were it desired in the future to make these changes.
Certain cabinet ministers talk about guaranteed annual income and all sorts of similar programs. With a fixed basic exemption, it becomes all the more difficult to introduce that type of system. For that reason, it would seem to me it would have been preferable to move toward something that is more flexible, and that is a tax credit system. Second, the change of exemption has proven to be an exceedingly difficult proposition. Ever since I have been in this House I have heard propositions about change in the level of personal exemption for taxpayers under the Income Tax Act. It has taken 22 years-as a matter of fact 23 years because we are dealing with the Income Tax Act of 1948-to make those changes. I suppose, going on the premise of past experience, it may take another 20 years before a further change is introduced. We are introducing a further degree of inflexibility in the income tax system which I think we could well eliminate. Therefore, I feel that the tax credit system again would be of advantage. Third, there is no doubt that the basic exemption is of greater value at marginal rates to the higher revenue earner than it is to the lower income earner. That is all there is to it.
To me there would seem to be a lack of logic in insisting upon this level of $1,500 and $1,350 per annum. I think the parliamentary secretary was frankly trying to engage in a useless comparison in talking about Great Britain, France, the United States and others in respect of the basic rate. It is the same as making a comparison of assessments or taxes in various Canadian cities because you can have high assessments and low tax rates or you can have low assessemnts and very high mill rates. The same thing applies here. We could have a very low exemption allowance but much higher rates initiating tax, yielding roughly the same thing and, so far as the taxpayer is concerned, with about the same effect. So, what the parliamentary secretary had to say does not in any way contribute to a comparison of the two systems.
One thing that I noted also was that the parliamentary secretary had perhaps slipped into the pitfall of trying to compare the position of the single status taxpayer at his best possible position in Canada. I admit that the exemption is the same, but the tax rates are certainly not and if, inadvertently, he was trying to give the impression that the single status taxpayer in Canada was better off than

he was in other countries, then I think he is wrong because one has to remember that in Canada the provinces have the right to levy income tax, and many of them do. The same is true of several states in the Uhited States which levy income taxes, and to compare individuals you must put them in the same relevant position. Unfortunately, the white paper engaged in some real flim-flam when it was comparing high rate individuals in the U.S. with low rate individuals in Canada.
With regard to the amounts, I would say that $1,500 is an arbitrary figure; $1,800 can be an arbitrary figure, just as $1,400 was an arbitrary figure. They bear no relationship at all to the cost of living. But then, when we consider the $2,850 and take a couple who are receiving their old age security, the taxpayer of the two gets an additional allowance of $650, which puts him in at $3,500, and with $100 general deduction, it means about $3,600 of income which would be completely tax exempt. To relate that to various poverty levels is also a very relevant question because $3,600 in Toronto or in Ottawa is certainly not $3,600 in some small centre in rural Ontario, rural Quebec or elsewhere in the country. These are all relative levels, and it does mean that a person with $3,600 in certain areas could be much better off than one living, say, in the centre of Toronto where I think his position would be absolutely impossible.
I think the parliamentary secretary might want to answer this question. In the light of the fact that three of the provinces, and there may be a fourth one, have lowered the age of majority to 18-and we know that this is going to be the trend in the next three or four years-why does the Income Tax Act make that break at the age of 21, as it does for children at page 278? At page 278, section 109 (l)(d) we find the following:
For each child or grandchild of the individual who, during the year, was wholly dependent upon him for support and was
(i)	under 21 years of age,
(ii)	21 years of age or over and dependent by reason of mental
or physical infirmity,
Why should the division not be now at the age of 18 in the case of mental or physical infirmity? This is more in conformity with the status of an adult. I assume the status of an adult is at the age of 21 in this statute because that was the dividing line between minority and majority. It seems to me that we will have to look into this in order to conform because provincial statutes relating to income tax, and other statutes under provincial jurisdiction will have some effect upon the status of a person as a taxpayer. Yet there remains this question of 21. The act makes another break at the age of 16. This is presumably the age of entry into high school, and yet so many children go to high school at a younger age than 16. I do not know why the age of 16 is used, but it seems to me that we could make the situation so much simpler by having one break at the age of 18. There are very few people who go into post secondary education who are younger than 18. The great majority of them do so after they have reached that age, and yet the break is at 16.
Perhaps there is an explanation that escapes me outside that of pure inertia and of not thinking about this particular point. However, it seems to me that there should be a straight break now at the age of 18, and that a person over the age of 18 should be considered as an adult because
October 25, 1971

almost half of the population of the country are considered as adults at that age.
Now, I should like to move to some comments with regard to section 110 dealing with some of the deductions that are permitted. First of all, let us take the case of medical expenses. One change that has been made which has not been noticed too much is that, whereas under the present act if an individual has a private health plan, any medical expenses paid by that health plan as a result of illness of the taxpayer or of the taxpayer's dependents in excess of 3 per cent of the taxpayer's income qualify him for the benefit of the medical expense allowance, the present act under section 110 does not do that. It restricts very severely the amount that may now be claimed. One cannot now claim that expenses that are paid under a private medical insurance plan. You can only claim the amount of the premium under the 3 per cent provision for medical expenses which might allow the taxpayer to qualify for the allowance. Frankly, this change provides no real relief whatsoever; in fact quite the contrary.
Of course, it is also known that in those provinces where the employer makes a contribution to an annual premium, say, in British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario, the contribution of the employer is added to the income of the individual, but because that is for medicare the individual cannot claim any of the medical expenses paid at so-called public cost to arrive at the 3 per cent allowance. I am not arguing whether there should or should not be a deduction for medical expenses that are paid by a public plan. But what I am saying is that I think it is highly inequitable if the employer makes any contribution whatsoever to all or part of the cost of a medical plan, that should not also, on the basis of the provisions relating to contributions to a private plan, be deemed to be an expense. Why add it if you are going to charge it to him as income? It should also be allowed as an expense in arriving at the 3 per cent allowance. As usual, the Crown is taking it both ways and I fail to see the justification for it. It is completely unfair.
The individual's own contributions do not entitle him to anything. If he pays half of the fee for medicare he gets nothing for that, no allowance. If his employer pays part of his medicare fee it is added to his income, and if he participates, as many people do, in supplementary medical care schemes, the only thing he can draw benefit from here is the premium, not the medical expenses, and that is a complete repudiation of the principle of medical expense allowances. Of course, it is bitterly criticized by a number of the organizations that have made representations to the government.
