Mr. Chairman, I would like to address myself to the question of medical expenses. There are people in this country who now find themselves discriminated against. These are people who live in Ontario, or Alberta, or other provinces where the provincial governments have determined that they will make none or only a minimal contribution to the medical premium which is payable by the citizens in those provinces. The result is that people in those provinces are now faced with what appears to them to be a condition of hardship and injustice. If they are fortunate enough to be employed by someone who, under a collective agreement or voluntarily, pays a part of their medical care premium, then that contribution made by their employer is added to their income. On the other hand, any payment they make themselves in respect of all or part of the premium is in no way deductible at any stage in the computation of income tax.
It is not deductible in the basic computation of income, nor is it included as an element of medical expenses, as is the case with premiums that are paid for private coverage. I would hope that the spokesmen for the government can comment on the difficult and somewhat unfair position in which residents of this province are placed as compared with residents of other provinces in regard to the operation of medical plans in Canada, bearing in mind that all these plans are supported by all people as taxpayers, and that the differential positions which Canadians experience under the plans are not the result of anything they have done, but rather a result of decisions by provincial governments over which they apparently have no control.
The second point I would like to raise about medical expenses has been put to me very forcefully by a family in my constituency. These people have the experience of having children who suffer from what are called, broadly speaking, learning disabilities. The word dyslexia applies as a description of this particular ailment, which is a very serious one. At the present time in this province whatever public institutions there may be for the treatment of this type of disability, they are not really adequate to cope with the demands on this family, nor I am informed with the demands on other families in my constituency that have the same type of problem.
These children are under doctors' care. Whatever is done with them is done as a result of medical advice and medical direction. But, because of some odd quirk in the interpretation of our laws, both provincial and federal, this particular family finds itself in a position which I think is as absurd as it is unjust. The parents are compelled to pay what to them is an enormous amount of

October 25, 1971
Income Tax Act
money each month, something like $400 to $500, to maintain their children in a special institution so that they can receive the kind of treatment, plus training, which will enable them to become useful citizens. The health authorities of the province of Ontario have determined that this is not an expense which is covered under health insurance, and the tax authorities of the federal government have stated that this is not an expense which is deductible as a medical expense.
I am not going to attempt to go through the jurisprudence on this matter except to say that the citations contained in CCH and other tax texts are somewhat contradictory. I do not think we can leave a matter of this kind in any position where there is doubt as to the taxpayer's rights, or any doubt as to the taxpayer's capacity to do all that he may to improve the health of his family and to overcome what any reasonable person would consider to be a severe medical disability. I notice that there is some textual change, and I will not go into detail at this time, between the existing law and the law as proposed. I think it would be a wise thing for the government to give an assurance to this House and to people, whose children suffer from these special types of disabilities, that there will be recognition of these special circumstances and the treatment will be properly recognized as a medical expense.
The third point I wish to make about medical expenses is in regard to the restrictive wording of the present section 27 (1) (c) which as far as I can see is substantially carried forward in the proposed section 110 (1) (c). Again I have in mind a specific case which seems to indicate absurdity in the administration of the law.
Shortly after the last election, one of my constituents brought to my attention a difficulty which he encountered in his family. His wife had experienced a nervous breakdown, had been confined for some time to a mental institution and had finally been released. The conditions of release were that she should continue to receive outpatient psychiatric care and have proper provision for the maintenance of herself and her home by a competent person. The arrangements were made by her husband under the direction of her doctor. A great deal of expense was incurred in providing for what used to be called a practical nurse to look after this lady. Mr. Chairman, the House now has before it one of the most interesting clauses concerning personal income tax and exemptions prescribed by the act to allow people to keep as much as possible of their income to support their family decently.
The bill, particularly geared to personal income tax, has been attentively considered by labour organizations whose responsibility it is to defend the interests of their members. They have made their recommendations known to us and I believe it is our duty, at the present stage of consideration of the bill, to speak on behalf of those organizations and request, suggest that the government amend some clauses of the bill in order to take more specially into account the rights of individuals, primarily of those workers who do not receive high salaries and who therefore have to do some extra belt-tightening to keep within their budgets.
For example, I am thinking of a labourer who is single and who up to the passage of the new legislation was entitled to a basic exemption of $1,100, while this bill provides that it will be raised to $1,600. Now I consider the basic exemption of $1,600 as clearly insufficient due to the cost of living which keeps going up. In my opinion, a single person, whatever his age, should be granted a much higher basic exemption. I am also thinking of a 21 or 22-year old man who must earn his living and is also considering the possibility of establishing himself. If he is not given the opportunity of saving enough to fulfil his ambitions, he will be discouraged.
The same thing applies to married couples. The new provisions of clause 109 provide for a tax exemption of $2,850. This is obviously not enough if one takes into account the increase in the cost of living.
To come back to the basic exemption, either for married couples or for single people, representations are often made to us by mechanics, for example, who are working in garages and must necessarily buy tools and maintain them. The company which employs them can usually deduct the purchase of these tools as expenses and depreciate them according to a scale recognized by the

department. This is not the case for workers. However, the act provides for deductions of employment expenses up to $150 a year. Mechanics are not rare who work in garages and own up to $2,000, $3,000 or $4,000 worth of tools that must be renewed periodically in order for them to accomplish their work in a suitable way.
It would be absolutely normal that those classes of workers be granted a basic exemption much greater in order to put them on a par with companies.

Mr. Chairman, in my contribution earlier today, I raised a point concerning the matter of tax reform for. those individuals who live together but are not in the category of married persons as defined by the present legislation, as contemplated by the new legislation or dealt with in the taxation courts. I did not receive a response, either reasoned or otherwise, from the parliamentary secretary. Somebody has to speak for them and somebody has to get an answer. I am going back to the subject again.
There are two such categories of people involved. These may be people who are quite free to marry, both having single status, but who have decided they are not going to marry and simply live together. That is called a common-law marriage. The other category is comprised of men and women who decide to live together because either one or both are not free to marry. In the eyes of the law they are really a concubine and paramour, but the parlance of the times that applies to them is the phrase living together common-law. I think we should recognize the status of these people. I do not think our Income Tax Act is a statute of morality. If anyone thinks it is, he should examine the actions of the income tax collector. When he finds that someone is plying the trade or profession of prostitution, that woman's earnings are quickly taxed, despite the fact she earns them in an immoral way.
We are not enacting a statute of morality. What we are trying to do is bring tax reform, tax justice and tax equity to all Canadians. A man and woman who have not entered into the bonds of matrimony may be living together in a community. Perhaps they have come from some other part of the country where, either or both have had an unhappy marriage. It is unjust unless we accord to them the same tax exemptions as we do to those who have gone through orthodox marriage ceremonies. I do not see where there would be any great harm in adopting a position such as that. I do not think it would cause the income tax people any great difficulties. Heaven knows, they find out about these things. I have had people come to me after the income tax people established that they were not in fact married, and all hell broke loose on their heads and shoulders. It always burned me up when something like that happened.
I ask the parliamentary secretary to now give me an answer. Perhaps he is taking it up with his advisers. If I do not get an answer now, I shall be asking the parliamen-
[The Deputy Chairman.]
tary secretary the same question a good number of times. The question is simply this. Why is it not possible, and I cannot do it, for some draftsman to take section A and enlarge the definition of a married person because we are dealing with the equivalence of married people in the two categories I mentioned. I refer to those people who are free to marry but who, for some reason choose not to do so, but live together as man and wife. The relationship is that of concubine and paramour and, although not properly, is usually called common-law, marriage. The other situation is that in which one or the other cannot marry, but they live together as man and wife. Why cannot the exemption be extended to both these categories?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I apologize to the hon. member. I did not intentionally omit responding to his question the last time. I covered a number of points. I ommitted reference to it accidentally.
The problem is one of administration, not in any strict sense of the word, but rather in the establishment of the common-law relationship to which the hon. member referred. I am sure the government agrees the taxing statute is not a place where moral sanctions are applied or moral rewards are handed out. In his comments, the hon. member at least intruded an element of morality to bring out the point. He referred to paramour and concubine. This presupposes that the couple are at least of the same sex, yet today that is not necessarily the situation that prevails. What are we to do about these things? How do you prove what is a common-law relationship? What is a common-law relationship that the tax assessor should take into account in deciding whether the marriage exemption should be granted? Is it a transitional relationship of a day or two or a week or two? What precisely is a common-law relationship to which the hon. member referred?
The hon. member distinguished two categories in this particular unchurched or unendorsed situation. One is where the couple are not, because of some other legal impediment, able to get married. In the other case he cited, the couple is free to marry, but do not do so. My reaction to that is very much like the reaction which we encountered in attempting to extend the small business incentive to unincorporated businesses. I am sorry we did not find a way to do it. On the other hand, the option of incorporation is open to most small businesses. Similarly, in this case, the option of matrimony is open to most taxpayers.
What an option.

Mr. Chairman, I want to resume my earlier remarks with regard to sections 109 and 110. There is one point I missed in section 109 that I would like to cover. If we look at the section dealing with dependents under personal exemptions, we find that some people are going to have an awful shock. For example, the old age supplement is no longer included for purposes of taxation. May I refer to the deductions that are permitted under section 110 at the top of page 286 of the bill:
(f) the amount of any supplement under the Old Age Security Act or of any similar payment under a law of a province, in

respect of which any amount has been included in computing the taxpayer's income for the year by virtue of clause 56(l)(a)(i)(A).
I may say that the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Canada have made the point that instead of using this alpha-numeric system it would have been far better to adopt the metric or decimal system of numbering paragraphs. I think that point is a good one and would have left the bill in far better shape. I am sure many people who have been trained as chartered accountants would adopt that suggestion of their professional society.
In any event, all of the income limitations of dependants operate to eliminate the allowance entirely when income reaches $1,600. Because the old age pension supplement is now included in a dependant's income, even though it is not taxable, a recipient on maximum supplement will not qualify as a dependant. Even though this money is not taxable but is deemed to be put in a special category, a dependant within the category prescribed by section 109- who is not a wife, that is-will not qualify as a dependant because the old age supplement will take him beyond the allowable amount. I think the parliamentary secretary should furnish an answer as to why this provision was made.
Reverting to section 110, under charitable donations we see a change in that the amount that has been allowed has gone from 10 per cent to 20 per cent of income. I think this is a very good move and will be generally applauded throughout the country. The organizations to which deductible donations may be made have been broadened in scope to include registered Canadian amateur athletic associations, though these must be of a national character. I think this will also bring us up against difficulties in interpretation; or, shall I say, some people will be terribly disappointed.
Although there has been an extension of charitable donations and individuals can benefit to the extent that the allowance has been increased from 10 per cent to 20 per cent of income, and although the gift tax is being eliminated, there is still one gate that has to be passed through that does not let off the gift scot free. I refer to the proposed capital gains tax. Even though a gift to a charitable organization may come within the 20 per cent level of income, if it falls within a category on which would be levied a capital gains tax then either the donor or even the recipient charitable organization would be liable for capital gains tax.
I think we should see to it that there is a general awareness of this provision. It has been represented directly to the government on behalf of charitable organizations that the provision will work to their detriment because under the capital gains tax provision a gift is deemed to be a sale and if there is an accretion in value it may be caught under that provision. I just want to make sure that that is understood.
There is one advantage of which I would have hoped the draftsmen of Bill C-259 would have availed themselves, and that is the elimination of subparagraphs (iii) to (xv) of section 110(l)(c). This was the old paragraph 27(l)(c) and some of its provisions. These provisions have become very awkward in that they are difficult to define and cause a great deal of difficulty in interpretation. It would have been preferable had the draftsmen followed the recommendation of the Canadian Institute of Chartered
Income Tax Act
Accountants and simply substituted for subparagraphs (iii) to (xv) inclusive the following provision: "(iii) For such expenses as may be prescribed by regulation". For example, subparagraph (xii) of section 110(l)(c) provides: for any device or equipment, not described in any other subparagraph of this paragraph, of a prescribed kind-
In other words, the provision allows for discretion if the device or equipment is prescribed by a physician, and it seems to me it would have been far better to take all the provisions detailed between pages 282 and the middle of page 284 into the regulatory field.
Having said that, within the same section I should like to turn to subparagraph (iv) which appears on page 282. It provides:
as remuneration for one full-time attendant upon, or for the fulltime care in a nursing home of, the taxpayer, his spouse or any such dependant who was throughout the whole of a 12 months' period ending in the taxation year necessarily confined by reason of illness, injury or affliction to a bed or a wheel chair-
At the present time there is difficulty in interpreting those words. Some assessment officers indicate that a taxpayer or a dependant must be confined to bed for a period of 12 months prior to entry into a nursing home if any nursing home expenses during that twelve months in the taxation year are to be claimed or allowed. I have heard another version in this regard, to the effect that there must be one entire 12-month period of confinement in the nursing home. Of course, I think that is wrong. I should like the parliamentary secretary to confirm what is meant by the language of this provision we are being asked to pass.
It seems to me that the logical interpretation of these words is that if a person is confined to bed or a wheel chair for a period of time and has spent some time in a nursing home, the total of which two periods is 12 months, that represents the 12-month period in a taxation year and is sufficient to qualify that person for an exemption of the expenses incurred.
Before I sit down I should like the parliamentary secretary to tell us whether there is a possibility of the government introducing further amendments after we pass these two sections. As the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants has asked, are there any changes to be made in addition to those forecast by the minister a week ago Thursday? If there are, I suggest we should leave these sections open. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in the first place it would be rather presumptuous of the government to assume that we have now heard all the representations of hon. members on the other side and are able to say we have in mind what additional amendments are to be proposed. Mr. Chairman, in dealing with sections 109 and 110, which concern personal exemptions for income tax purposes, I wish to make two points. My first point relates to the general level of exemptions provided by the proposed legislation, in that they are not high enough, and the second is that the government in proposing this legislation should have gone to a tax credit system rather than continuing a tax exemptions system.
In keeping with the customary logic of this House, perhaps I should deal with the first point first, that is, the general levels of exemptions proposed in this bill. It will not take much time to go over this point because it was dealt with extensively by a number of members on second reading of the bill and during the general discussion on clause 1.
Perhaps at the outset I should say that section 109 (1) (h) is generally acceptable to us in the NDP. The section proposes that the deduction from income for elderly taxpayers 65 years of age and over be $650, with the guaranteed income supplement being exempt, whereas formerly the $500 additional exemption was available if the taxpayer was aged 70 or over. We consider that to be an improvement and we are especially pleased to note that it ends the anomaly of taxing pensioners on their income from the guaranteed income supplement, knowing they had to go through a means test to get it in the first place. This situation would have been laughable if it had not been so tragic in its consequences. The government said, on the one hand, that a pensioner could not live on less than $135 per month but, on the other hand, taxed a portion of that amount. We welcome the end of this situation when the legislation passes.
Section 109 (1) (d) deals with exemptions for wholly or partly dependent children. That section proposes that for each dependent child under 16, and children up to 21 years of age who are totally dependent by reason of infirmity or attending school or university, a deduction of $300 can be made. This deduction is reduced $1 for every $2 of a child's income over $1,000. Formerly the provision was that if the income was over $950, the excess could be added to the parents' tax. Section 109 (1) (d) (v) proposes

that for dependent children over 16 the deduction from income be $550, which is reduced by $1 for every $1 of the child's income over $1,050. The former provision was that a parent could deduct $550, and if the child's income was over $950 the excess might be added to the parents' tax.
The changes have not altered the exemptions in any substantial fashion. There is an air of unreality surrounding them. They bear no more relationship to the costs of rearing and educating a child than they did formerly. The new regulations may bring marginal relief to some families, but it is so marginal that one wonders why the government even bothered to undertake this somewhat more elaborate formula. As I said at the outset, I do not intend to go into the arguments extensively because it has been done time and time again. The point to be made is simply that the exemption provided for wholly or partially dependent children bears no relationship to the actual cost of maintaining these children.
Turning to personal exemptions, section 109 (1) (a) proposes that the deduction from income for a married couple be $2,850, increased from $2,000, and section 109 (1)
(c)	proposes that the deduction from income for a single person be $1,500, increased from $1,000. Personal exemptions should not be figures which are simply picked out of the air. They must relate to something, and surely that something is the amount of money it takes a Canadian to live on at a level which does not entail poverty.
The Economic Council of Canada has suggested that a single person in Canada earning less than approximately $2,000 a year is living below the poverty line, and that a married couple earning less than approximately $4,000 a year is living below the poverty line. Surely, then, $2,000 and $4,000 are the logical levels at which to fix personal exemptions so as to ensure that no one is forced to contribute to the general well-being of the community through taxes at the cost of being forced to live in poverty. I wish the government had given this factor more consideration in computing the level at which they would fix personal exemptions.
Another means of considering the adequacy of personal exemption levels is to compare them to increases in the cost of living. We find that between September, 1949, the last time personal exemptions were increased, and September of this year the cost of living for Canadians, in constant dollars, has risen by approximately 125 per cent, whereas the proposed increase in personal exemption is only approximately 42 per cent. There is an obvious disparity here.
Another way to look at it is to consider the annual average income of Canadians. In 1949 the personal exemption was fixed at $1,000 for a single person, and the average income was about $900. The personal exemption was considerably above the average income. Now the average income far exceeds the exemption. The other point to be made with regard to the proposed exemptions and the new rate schedules is that they result in greater savings in dollars for those with larger incomes. I might illustrate that by comparing the tax saving from the increased exemption which would be realized by people at different income levels.
October 25, 1971

With a gross income of $2,000, the tax saving from the increased exemption with the new rate schedule to a single taxpayer with no dependants would be $33. With a gross income of $4,000, it would be $160. At $6,000 the saving would be $177; at $8,000 it would be $195; at $15,000 it would be $258; at $50,000 it would be $364; and at $100,000 it would be $397. So the annual tax saving increases as a person's income increases. That is why we say we should have gone to a tax credit system. The parliamentary secretary said it would not be simple to implement. No one denies that. All that need be said in rebuttal, I submit, is that neither is a system of exemptions simple to implement and that the effort required to overcome difficulties in a system of tax credits, if greater, also has much greater pay-offs in terms of equity, in terms of the flexibility introduced into the tax system and in terms of offsetting the effects of somewhat regressive forms of taxation such as customs duties and sales taxes which bear almost equally on all Canadians.
Both the tax credit and the tax exemption are designed to recognize that a certain portion of an individual's income should be free of tax. The exemption specifically states the amount of income which should not be subject to tax. Under the present system it is $1,000 for a single taxpayer and in the proposed legislation it would be $1,500. But because we have in Canada what is technically called a progressive rate schedule, increases in exemptions generally benefit higher income earners, as the figures I cited a few moments ago illustrate.
The tax credit system does not state the amount of income that should be exempt but states an amount of tax that need not be paid, a set sum which can be deducted from a citizen's total tax bill, and thus gives each citizen the same monetary benefit. Thus, the tax credit would give greater relief to lower income groups, which surely is what a tax system should attempt to accomplish. The fact that the government has not gone to a system of tax credits in this legislation is but one more piece of evidence that this country is run in the interest of the upper income levels of the middle-class to the exclusion of benefits for the lower income groups.
Tp illustrate that point further, the same is true of the recently proposed 3 per cent reduction in income tax and the earlier removal of the 3 per cent surcharge. Both these measures have the effect of giving the greatest dollar relief to upper income earners and not lower income earners. By this process the government is attempting to generate greater activity in the economy. If greater benefit were given to the low income workers, the effect on the economy would be greatest because due to their income position they would spend virtually all their income. In the upper income groups, because they would save a portion of their money the immediate effect on the economy would probably be less.
Faced with difficulties in respect of the economy, the government came up with what amounts to a $1 billion bonanza for the upper income groups and corporations and at the same time argues that it is not able to implement a system of guaranteed annual income because such a system would cost $2 billion or $2.6 billion a year to operate, if the figures of the Economic Council of Canada are to be accepted.
Income Tax Act
I venture to say that recent tax cuts together with the removal of the surcharge represent the largest portion of revenue necessary to implement a guaranteed annual income, if we accept the figures of the Economic Council of Canada, and that a guaranteed annual income would provide greater stimulation to the economy than would the tax cuts, despite that being their ostensible purpose. Similarly, a system of tax credits would generally benefit most greatly the lower income groups. That is the major reason we in the New Democratic Party argue the need for the implementation of such a system. Meaningful tax reform means meaningful redistribution of income, and the proposed changes in exemption levels simply will not accomplish that end. Redistribution of income is something to which government in this country must address itself in the very near future.

Mr. Chairman, one is at a disadvantage when the only person one can preach to is out of the chamber. The parliamentary secretary is now returning, so I will make my point.
I have been pleading throughout the day for justice for a sizeable number of people who live together but are not married to each other. Each of these couples consists of two persons, and one is invariably a man and the other one is invariably a woman, despite some misunderstanding on the other side. Perhaps they do not tell things with the niceties of distinction that we do on this side. In any event, I suggested, and the parliamentary secretary agreed with me, that our taxing statute should not be a moral statute, that we are really not concerned with that here; we are concerned with fairness toward all. The parliamentary secretary, having agreed with me, said that people living together who are free to get married should get married. Who points the moral finger there and wags it about?
Regarding the other category of those who live together but are not free to marry each other, the parliamentary secretary said they would be few in number. There are estimates presented by welfare councils in Canada that up to 200,000 people are in that category, a group that would populate a city larger the Halifax and one a little smaller than that from which the parliamentary secretary comes. So we are dealing with sizeable numbers of Canadians. I suggest, again, that a formula could be reached so that they would receive exactly the same benefits, no more no less, than those of us who have gone through the marriage ceremony.
The parliamentary secretary also made the point that there might be some young Lothario who would take unto himself a different girl every year for purposes of income tax exemptions and relief. I thought that probably there

would not be people so bold, but perhaps there are. But then I said to myself: So what? What difference does it make if he supports a different woman every year of his life? If he is that kind of optimist, let him do it so long as he is not claiming two or more women for exemptions.
Oh, oh!

I can hear the hooting and hollering starting, Mr. Chairman, because one tries to fight for a minority that cannot possibly represent itself in this chamber. It is then that the baying hounds over there must yap and have their fun. That will keep the debate going longer, gentlemen, because I will stay with this point until hell freezes over and until we get some kind of satisfactory answer from the government.
Hear, hear!

What they are saying is that it would be a lot of work to check on some of these people, therefore let us not do it, let us see to it that they pay a disproportionate share of income tax because otherwise it would interfere with that great god that the Liberals worship- administrative efficiency. I say that that is also a weakness in their argument. But this whole exercise has also raised in the first few hours of the debate something that is very wrong with the section. We are being asked to pass one of the most important measures that any Parliament can pass and certainly the most important measure that this Parliament is being asked to pass, and that is a new Income Tax Act.
One would think that for that sort of occasion we would have someone here who is responsible to the House of Commons. But we have the parliamentary secretary. He is an estimable chap, but any suggestions that we make to him here and that we make to his officials-they are not the government, they are not the cabinet-they can slough off with a yes or a no, generally a no. That has been the performance so far today.
I say that is irresponsible. Because of the importance of this legislation the Minister of Finance should be in his seat for every moment of the debate, listening if possible but at least present so that we may ask questions and get proper answers instead of what we have received so far, a series of remarkably inept answers. I say this with all deference to the parliamentary secretary. I have respect for him, but after some of this stuff all I can say is that if he is passing on what his advisers tell him, he had better get new advisers; or if he is passing on what he himself knows, he had better get out and find out something about the domestic law of Canada.
I put the question again. I am asking as seriously and as responsibly as I can, on behalf of people not able to ask it themselves, that the definition of "married person" be broadened in section 109(a), line 2, so that the people I have mentioned, who are not married but who live together as man and wife, may have the benefit of the income tax legislation we are being asked to enact.

Mr. Chairman, the following appeared in Le Devoir of December 27, 1968:

The Canadian Prime Minister, Mr. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, in his Christmas message to the people, asks them to co-operate with the government, during the coming year, in its efforts to reduce social inequalities.
"Our country," the Prime Minister stated, "is one of the most beautiful in the world, one of the most peaceful and one of the most affluent."
"But it has its problems and its difficulties. Some of our citizens do not partake as much as they should of the general welfare of the country. Some others do not enjoy the same freedoms and privileges as the majority of Canadians."
"It is therefore imperative," the message goes on, "to reduce those inequalities, and it is our intention to work relentlessly towards this end during the coming year."
"But to achieve those objectives," he added, "we need the cooperation of all citizens, we need their goodwill, which must always be stronger than any ill will, so that, together, we may ensure in a peaceful manner, the welfare of everyone and the progress of the whole country."
Mr. Chairman, those were very pious wishes expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). In fact, he intended to reform and to cure what he thought was the cause of a certain uneasiness.
Judging from various reports and studies, we may wonder what was the result of the appeal launched by the Prime Minister with a view to levelling social inequalities and determining the extent of the co-operation of welfare recipients, of lower income groups, of businessmen, of industrialists who must close down their factories, of tradesmen who go bankrupt.
The call for co-operation from all Canadians went too far, in my opinion, since the unbalance we experience actually and which is labelled by experts under the terrifying name of inflation is in fact nothing but the unreasonable shifting of purchasing power in the hands of the various sectors of society. Indeed there is inflation in the upper echelons of society and deflation in the less favored ones.
From the Prime Minister down to the latest newborn this year, we are all governed by money requirements in order to meet our personal, familial and social needs.
We need just as much money to live as we need the air we breathe. Clause 109 of Bill C-259 now under study is somewhat disturbing, since it does not fully recognize human needs. In fact, clause 109 on page 277 of the bill reads:
(1) For the purpose of computing the taxable income of an individual for a taxation year, there may be deducted from his income for the year such of the following amounts as are applicable:
(a) in the case of an individual who, during the year, was a
married person who supported his spouse, an amount equal to
the aggregate of
(i)	$1,500, and
(ii)	$1,350 less the amount, if any, by which the spouse's income
for the year while married exceeds $250;
Mr. Chairman, at first sight, these proposals seem quite interesting, but they are clearly inadequate when we look at the consumer index for September 1971, for instance, which has reached 134.5 related to the basic year 1961.
If we take the year 1949 as the basic year, that is the year basic tax exemptions had been fixed, this index has now reached 174. As a matter of fact, the basic exemptions whose amount had been fixed in 1949 have never been reviewed, which leads us to believe that the workers
October 25, 1971

have really been forgotten by the governments that have succeeded one another until now, and we find that the proposed increase provided in clause 109 of Bill C-259 is much below the increase in consumer prices.
Indeed, in the case where single people are concerned the exemption will be increased from $1,000 to $1,500 and in the case of married people without children it will be increased from $2,000 to $2,850. Thus we have recuperated 24 per cent in the first case and 31 per cent in the second case.
Simultaneously, our national production has increased fourfold. The assets of our chartered banks have increased sixfold. The stocks and shares of the 800 largest Canadian corporations have increased seventeenfold. And the salaries of the members of this House have been multiplied by 4.
In view of such inequities it seems to me that we must find solutions in order to correct this situation. We must not only bring the exemptions up to a level which will allow total recovery, but go beyond that level if we really want to alleviate the tax burden of the small and average taxpayers.
We must keep in mind that so far the increase in the cost of living has affected taxpayers in the low income bracket more, since the items for which prices have increased most are essentials-that is, food, clothing, and housing.
Above all, we must remember, in reference to this bill- and particularly to clause 109-that the revenues of all levels of government from personal income tax have increased from 20.6 per cent in 1961 to 31.5 per cent in 1971, which represents an 11 per cent increase.
The Economic Council of Canada stated in its 1968 report that the poverty line was situated at $2,000 for single people, and $3,500 for married couples without children.
Now, those figures are all higher than the basic exemptions suggested by the Minister of Finance. So, to remedy the situation, and because I want to respond to the right hon. Prime Minister who said that they needed the cooperation of all the citizens, I bring in my contribution this evening by moving the following amendment:
That Bill C-259 be amended by deleting from subparagraph (ii) of paragraph (a) of subclause (1) of clause 109 the figure "$1,350" and substituting therefor the figure "$2,500".

At this point, prima facie I would agree with his ruling, but I would not want to deprive hon. members of the opportunity to make submissions.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few comments.
During the recess, I perused certain documents which lead me to believe that, according to the way the Standing Orders are interpreted in connection with moving of the amendment, there would not be any additional expenses
Income Tax Act
entailed by the government nor any new taxes for the taxpayers.
Citation 265 of the 4th edition of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms has been quoted. It reads as follows:
No member other than a minister of the Crown may introduce a Bill for the reduction of duties. The government must take full responsibility for the taxation levied to provide the revenue. But the House enjoys complete freedom to make every representation possible to the Government with regard to the manner in which the ministers discharge this responsibility.
And it is added
This duty the members may perform by moving amendments to reduce the taxes proposed by the Administration.
Now, later the following can be read in comment 269:
-nor would any amendment to extend the imposition of a tax to persons enjoying an exemption therefrom be now permitted.
The objective here is not to extend taxes to another group, but to exempt certain people from a tax under Bill C-259.
I believe that the legislator sought, by way of that rule, to retain for the government the power to introduce fiscal legislation in Parliament.
Indeed, the matter was debated right here in the House of Commons on May 22, 1941 and the then Speaker delivered a ruling on an amendment brought forward on the occasion of the introduction of a bill seeking to increase the tax on gazoline to 3 cents. An hon. member had then presented an amendment tending to increase the tax to 4 cents. That was therefore a tax increase resulting from a private member's motion. The Speaker's ruling was put to the vote and upheld by the House, which is quite understandable to me.
Now, though I have made some quick research during recess, I could not find in our Standing Orders anything which forbids a member to expresse himself concretely in this House while introducing an amendment which would be such as to protect the taxpayers from an excessive tax burden.
In view of these circumstances, since we are considering the productive capacity of our vast country, and based on logical reasoning, it is possible for Canada to decrease the tax burden of certain categories of Canadians who, in our opinion, are overtaxed. So, we assume that we have the privilege to introduce an amendment for this purpose so as to urge this government to increase the basic exemption.
There, Mr. Chairman, are the few remarks that I wanted to bring to your attention before you make your decision.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. If no other hon. members would like to assist the Chair, if hon. members would bear with me I think it might be helpful if I were to outline as briefly as I can the principles applicable to the procedural acceptability of this motion. I think I might be justified in doing that because of the remarks just made by the hon. member for Bellechasse. I appreciate that there is in his mind and in the minds of other hon. members some question about the basis for the procedural acceptability of this motion.

October 25, 1971
Income Tax Act
The first consideration might be the rule of relevancy, and I would be of the opinion that the proposed amendment does not offend that rule. Second, there is the principle that no member may propose an amendment to increase taxation or extend its incidence. Again, I am of the opinion that the amendment now before the committee does not offend either aspect of the principle I have just stated. Indeed, the proposal before the Chair goes in the opposite direction in that it would have the effect not only of reducing that aspect of taxation, as the hon. member pointed out in his argument, but it would also restrict the incidence of the tax by eliminating taxation for a substantial number of persons who would be taxpayers under the proposal now found in the bill. On those first two principles I have no disagreement with hon. members who have argued that this motion is procedurally acceptable.
The third principle, however, that of the financial initiative of the Crown in relation to money and taxation proposals, gives the Chair some difficulty. I might, for example, ask hon. members who have argued either this afternoon or this evening whether this sort of motion is procedurally acceptable and whether they would suggest that as private members they could do something indirectly by means of an amendment such as this which they could not do directly by way of a bill. I would think the answer would be in the negative. I do not think it would be argued that a private member could amend, for example, the Income Tax Act by way of a bill.
It seems to me that it would matter little that the financial initiative of the government permits it to initiate a taxation proposal if it were then open to any member to propose, by way of amendment, a different substantive scheme of his own, and I think that is the situation the Chair has before it.
It seems to me that the proposition put forward by the hon. member for Portneuf does not amend the proposal put forward by the government it would, I suggest, supplant, rather than amend, the government's proposal. In effect, he would suspend the initiative of the Crown in taxation measures and thereby bring about a fundamental change in the financial procedures of this House. In his argument the hon. member referred to Beauchesne's Fourth Edition, citation 265. He made a very strong argument. However, it is important to distinguish between the matters which have been raised. Citation 265(1) of Beauchesne's Fourth Edition reads:
No member other than a minister of the Crown may introduce a bill for the reduction of duties. The government must take full responsibility for the taxation levied to provide the revenue. But the House enjoys complete freedom to make every representation possible to the government with regard to the manner in which the ministers discharge this responsibility. This duty the members may perform by moving amendments to reduce the taxes proposed by the administration.
As I understand the hon. member's argument, he is relying strongly on the words: "This duty the members may perform by moving amendments to reduce the taxes proposed by the administration." I would accept that citation as being binding upon the Chair and agree with that part of the hon. member's argument. If I may use an example, the hon. member would be free to move an
[The Chairman.]
amendment to reduce the rate of taxation from 10 per cent, say, to 9 per cent, if that would affect all taxpayers across the board.
If the hon. member could fit his proposal within that citation, the Chair, being bound by the citation, would have to accept it. However, I have to distinguish that situation from the motion. According to the motion, the hon. member is proposing that some taxpayers be relieved of the payment of taxes and this is where the fundamental difference comes in. According to the citation to which hon. members have referred and I have just read, it would be permissible for hon. members to reduce taxation across the board. That is what the citation says. By his motion the hon. member is proposing to reduce taxes for some Canadians, undoubtedly, and to eliminate taxation for others.
It seems to me that is the crux of the matter and on this distinction I have to base my decision. It would matter little that the government could initiate a taxation proposal if it were then open to any member to propose, by way of amendment, a substantive and overriding scheme of his own. With respect, I think that is what the hon. member has proposed. He is substituting a substantively different scheme for the scheme which is in the bill before the committee. I thank the hon. member for his very valuable argument; however, for the reasons I have given I must rule that the motion is not procedurally admissible.

Mr. Chairman, the provisions increasing exemptions from $1,000 to $1,500 for single people and from $2,000 to $2,850 for married couples are among the most mean, niggardly, unfair, unjust and inequitable parts of this bill.
What about scandalous? That's a good word.

There are other sections which could be described in the same way, Mr. Chairman. However, the section referred to applies to so many Canadians of the lower income brackets that I feel impelled to speak on their behalf. When one considers that the basic, single person exemption was set at $1,000 in 1949 and that 22 years later it is to be increased to $1,500, and when one takes into account the tremendous increase in the cost of living since 1949, is it any wonder that I call this provision mean, niggardly, unfair, unjust and inequitable?
Don't repeat all that again.

Mr. Chairman, when I remember what Mr. Carter said about tax exemptions-he preferred tax credits to replace them-I submit that if Mr. Carter were present this evening he would ask us strongly and forcefully to implement his ideas. An exemption of $1,500 for a single person means that any person earning over $30 a week will be taxed. An exemption of $2,850 means that any married couple earning over $55 a week will be taxed. Any married man earning more than that will pay tax.
Mr. Chairman, we tested the Minister of Finance a few months ago after he said during a radio broadcast that a single man could live on $30 a week. The hon. member for Winnipeg North brought forward a motion asking the minister to live on that amount of money for a time and then report back to the House. Of course, the idea was
October 25, 1971

rejected because the minister and members on the Liberal side knew it was totally impossible for a single person to live on $30 a week. Yet when it comes to exemptions, that is what we do. As a result of these proposed changes, a single person earning over $30 a week will be taxed and a married person earning over $55 a week will be taxed.
One of the shortcomings of a democracy is that members on the government side must vote in support of government legislation. Try to picture the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton, a minister of the church, attempting to sell the principle in his riding of a $1,500 exemption for single persons. He would not succeed, Mr. Chairman. However, as a member of the Liberal party he is bound to support the government, to accept the proposal and to vote against any amendment which would increase the exemption.
Picture the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville, who represents a workingman's riding, attempting to persuade the people of his area that the $1,500 single persons' exemption is acceptable. He could not do it. Yet because we live under a democratic system the hon. member, if he supports his party, will vote for that exemption. There ought to be a free vote on this section because there are on the Liberal side many members whose hearts must ache and who must cringe when they consider that the government is increasing personal exemptions from $1,000 to $1,500 for single people, and so on. I cannot imagine even the worst Liberal, so to speak, supporting this type of increased exemption.
I notice the hon. member for Scarborough West, who is now a parliamentary secretary, pointing his finger at me and probably saying, "No, John, you are wrong." I ask him to take this bill to his riding and ask his people whether an exemption level which was set at $1,000 in 1949 is acceptable at $1,500 in 1971. Is that exemption level acceptable to the people who voted for him in 1968? I am sure, knowing his honesty and fairness, that he would say, "Of course it is not." Yet he is bound by his party to vote for this provision.
The very least we should do is increase the personal exemption from $1,000 to $2,000 for single people and from $2,850 to $4,000 for married couples. What does this mean, Mr. Chairman? If we increase the exemption to $2,000 for a single person he will then have to pay income tax on income over $40 a week. A married person will have to pay tax on income over $80 a week. I ask Your Honour and the members of this House how a single person can live on $40 a week and a married couple can live on $80 a week in today's world. It just is not realistic when one takes into account the high rents and cost of living that we have today.
The Economic Council of Canada underlined to this government what it means to live below the poverty line. They said the minimum amount required for a single person in 1968 was $1,850. They would now say the minimum should be $2,000 for a single person. They said at that time a married couple would require at least $3,200. Now they would say they require $4,000. Yet this government wants a segment of Canada to live below the poverty line. They want to impose tax on a single person who earns more than $1,500, and $2,850 for a married couple.

The member for Sault Ste. Marie comes from a workingman's family. He has done quite well in his profession. He was elected by the ordinary folk in that city. I am sure he feels ashamed this evening when discussing the exemptions the government has proposed. If he went back to his constituency and conducted a poll with regard to these exemptions, I am sure his people would object to them. I am surprised that the member for Sault Ste. Marie, who is a workingman's son and has worked himself, sits idly by, lets this section ride and will support the government on it.
Shame!

The Minister of National Health and Welfare has made speeches in the past few weeks with regard to the guaranteed annual income. At times he has attempted to protect the unemployed. I admire him for his courage because at this time in our welfare state, which in many ways has been created by the Liberal government and has caused much heartache and divisiveness in the country, he is trying to protect the unemployed. The minister comes from the city of Hamilton where many people are unemployed and many are earning very low incomes. How can he justify these miserably low exemptions of $1,500 for single people and $2,850 for married couples?
I hear a voice from the west, the member for St. Boniface. I am sure there are many French speaking people in his constituency. The province of Quebec also has high unemployment, poverty and many other problems. We are now attempting to straighten out those problems by giving this miserable, mean, despicable increase from $1,000 to $1,500 for single people and $2,000 to $2,850 for married couples. I am sure he is not very proud that he is not speaking for the French people in St. Boniface and the French people in the province of Quebec who have suffered unemployment and poverty as a result of this government's policies.

He said he would prefer to accept the message from St. Paul than to accept the message from St. Pat. I know it is very hard for the parliamentary secretary to accept this because he totally rejects the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Bruce. The truth hurts, Mr. Chairman, and it certainly hurts the Liberals in mid-section.
If we were to eliminate depletion allowances for natural resource industries and the three-year exemption with no offsetting provisions, we would add another $224.6 million. The argument of the hon. member for Bruce is that we cannot increase the personal exemption for a single person from $1,500 to $2,000 and for a married couple from $2,850 to $4,000 because it will cost $500 million. According to the argument of the Minister of Finance of Manitoba, by taking certain steps we can increase revenue by $3,000 million. So is it any wonder that the poor parliamentary secretary attempts to laugh off the argument and to shake his head and say that it cannot be done? Is it any wonder that I am striking this evening at some of the Liberals who come from ridings heavily populated by the working people? If they were to go back to their ridings and ask these people whether they are satisfied with the increase from $1,000 to $1,500 and from $2,000 to $2,850 at a time of high unemployment and high cost of living, there would be a total rejection of these exemptions.
I say that exemptions of $2,000 for a single person and of $4,000 for a married couple are the very minimum that this government should bring forward. I am sure some members will shake off their lethargy and when the times comes to vote on the section they will be men of courage, men of concern, men of compassion and will vote for the ordinary folk in the community rather than for the rich, fat-cats that support their party.

Mr. Chairman, I have the pleasure of saying a few words on clause 109 of the bill which concerns the vast majority of Canadian workers.
I am particularly concerned while studying this clause to note that the federal government always seems to be in agreement with the advice of those economists who are in favour of tax increases only. For example, when leading Canadian economists advocate tax cuts for all taxpayers, they are not listened to. Their recommendations seem not to be taken into account. The government apparently listens only to those who favour a continuous increase in taxes.
In Le Devoir of May 2, 1971, Canadian economists stated that:
Ottawa should reduce personal income tax and sales tax.
October 25, 1971

The government should reduce the personal income tax and the federal sales tax in order to stimulate productivity and slow down salary inflation, said economist Grant L. Reuber, Director of the Economics Department of Western University in London.
So, Mr. Chairman, here is an economist who demands tax reductions, but to whom the government, apparently, does not listen.
I continue with my quotation:
According to Mr. Reuber, the Bank of Canada has made Canada's economic problems more serious by going from one extreme to the other and by alternating between credit restrictions and capital flow into the banking system.
Further, Canadian taxes are traditionally high and American tax reductions could be used as a basis for radical changes in the tax system.
Here is an economist who is in favour of continued economic progress while at the same time asking for tax reductions. One tends to believe, when one is speaking to the government, when tax reductions are in question, that automatically they will entail a reduction in revenue for the government.
At this point, I should like to refer to a speech made on American television by a former president of the United States, and which was published in the "United States News Annual Report" of September 30, 1963.1 quote:

President Kennedy's address to the nation by radio and television, September 18,1963-
President's reasons for tax cuts-

If the then President of United States felt a tax cut in his country would be favourable to the Canadian as well as to the American economy as a whole, the same reasons prevail in 1971. These reasons which were put forward in the United States in 1963 might well be the same that would justify the Canadian government to cut taxes in 1971.

First: A tax cut means more jobs for American workers. More after-tax money means more buying power for consumers and investors-and this means more production and the jobs our nation needs. Merely to reduce unemployment to a more acceptable level in the next two and a half years, we must create more than 10,000 new jobs every day. We cannot effectively attack the problem of teenage crime and deliquency as long as so many of our young people are out of work. We cannot effectively solve the problem of racial injustice as long as unemployment is high. We cannot tackle the problem of automation when we are losing one million jobs every year to machines.
Second: A tax cut means new protection against another tragic recession. I do not say that a recession is inevitable without a tax cut, or impossible with one. But, excluding war years, we have had a recession on the average every 42 months since World War II-or every 44 months since World War I. And by next January, it will be 44 months since the last recession began. Recessions mean high unemployment and high budget deficits.
Mr. Chairman, when the federal government is on the point of showing a very high deficit, this points, as the President of United States stated in 1963, to an economic recession.

Of all kinds of waste, they are the worst. We need a tax cut to keep this present drive from running out of gas.
Income Tax Act
And third: A tax cut means new markets for American business. American citizens will spend, as history shows us, an overwhelming percentage of the extra after-tax dollars left in their pockets; and this spending will broaden markets for businessmen, put idle machines to work, and require new machines and new factories to be built-
Fourth: A tax cut means higher family income and higher business profit and a balanced federal budget.

That is inconsistent with what the hon. members opposite have seemingly believed for generations, namely, that a tax cut means less income for the federal government. [English]
A tax cut means higher family income and higher business profit and a balanced federal budget. Every taxpayer and his family will have more money left over after taxes for a new car, a new home, new conveniences, education and investments. Every businessman can keep a higher percentage of his profits in his cash register, or put it to work expanding or improving his business. And as the national income grows, the federal government will ultimately end up with more revenues.

This, Mr. Chairman, once more has not been understood by the government, I think.
I go on quoting:

Prosperity is the real way to balance our budget-

Mr. Chairman, prosperity is the only solution if we are to balance the budget.
I go on with the quotation:

Fifth and finally: A tax cut means new strength around the world for the American dollar and for freedom. A tax cut can help us balance our international accounts and end the outflow of gold by helping make the American economy more efficient and more productive and more competitive, by enabling our goods to compete with those who are developing foreign factories, and by making investments in America more attractive than investments abroad-
This nation needs a tax cut now-not a tax cut "if" and "when" but a tax cut now and for the future.

Mr. Chairman, those are the five reasons given by the president of the United States in 1963 to outline the economic policy to be followed in that country.

The hon. member has quoted the views of an economist which apparently have been published in Canadian newspapers in May 1971 and in American newspapers in 1963. Mr. Chairman, if I wanted to answer that question, I would have to ask the hon. member several others because his question is so impenetrable that it is difficult to understand it.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the data quoted in 1963 are quite the same as those that the economists have been quoting every day since the budget speech.
In fact, if we are to have a balanced budget, if we want our economy to remain alive, we need to have prosperity in Canada. Any intelligent man, any logical economist, favours prosperity in order to boost the economy and to allow the federal government to have a balanced budget- a great cause of worry for hon. members on the other side when we ask for tax reductions. This is precisely what the speaker before me did when he asked for a basic exemption of $3,000 for single people, and $5,000 for married couples. They think that the federal government would lose considerable revenues by granting such exemptions.
Considering we have thousands of unemployed in Canada and the economy is not progressing, the national treasury is losing very substantial revenues anyway.
Mr. Chairman, as the previous speaker said, today single Canadians will have to pay federal taxes the moment they earn a salary equivalent to $30 a week. For married people, the amount will be $57 a week. I am convinced those figures are totally illogical and unrealistic.
This is why we ask that the basic exemption be set at $3,000 for any single person and $5,000 for married persons.
Mr. Chairman, if we want to get our economy moving again, we must put an end to the inefficient administration of the country: we should avoid travelling the same financial and economic paths that have been trodden for more than 100 years in Canada. If we do not change our attitude in regard to the financial measures and the financial doctrine which the government, through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), seems to apply and according to which those who are well off should be gradually dispossessed, we will end up with a society of dispossessed people.
If we want to eradicate unemployment, we should create prosperity. We must provide incentives to those who wish to invest in Canada. The only reason for investing is capital gain. With the current budget or the tax reform of the Minister of Finance, we are about to elimi-The Deputy Chairman.)
nate private initiative in Canada, and this is no way to improve our competitiveness since one of our present problems is being unable to sell our production on world markets. Our production has become too costly, taxes are too high and when the private sector adds up its production costs retail prices are too high. We cannot compete with foreign countries.
If we want to keep our present share of both domestic and foreign markets, it is an absolute necessity for us to leave the beaten track of present orthodox finance so as to enable the Canadian economy to expand, to produce what we can produce, as we have the needed skill, manpower, equipment, raw materials and natural resources. This country is extraordinarily rich but our economic system is outdated. The taxation system no longer meets the needs of private enterprise.
Should we wish to establish an economic system by means of which the government would own. everything, should we wish to establish a socialist system, we need only to keep on smothering those who would like to see this country become great and prosperous.
I am always dismayed to see our hon. friends opposite ready to tax further private enterprise in Canada, to tax further the small wage earner, the worker by limiting the basic exemption to $30 a week for single persons and to $57 a week for married people.
Not more than six months ago, we had the opportunity-in this House to vote on salary increases for members of Parliament. We did not bother then to determine whether or not those increases would create a deficit in the budget of the hon. Minister of Finance, nor where the Minister of Finance would find the money. There was no discussion, apart from the opposition coming from this corner of the House.
It seems to me that when we speak on behalf of the population as a whole, of the majority of workers who have to work hard to feed their families, it is absurd in 1971 to talk about a basic exemption of $1,500 for single persons and $2,850 for married couples.
Mr. Chairman, I therefore support what my hon. colleagues submitted by way of amendments, and I hope that the government-not before the next elections but very soon-will reconsider these facts and listen to economists who do not always advocate tax increases but increased prosperity for Canada, which might perhaps mean the same revenues for the federal Treasury.

Mr. Chairman, this government reminds me of the farmer who had a horse. He had an idea one day that he could save money by taking away a handful of hay from the manger and that this would not make any difference to the horse. He decided the following day that if he took away two handfuls he would save more money in feeding the horse. He did this day after day, taking away one more handful each day. He was getting on very well. He was saving a nice pile of money. Unfortunately, the horse died.
Shame!

This farmer was so busy looking at the savings he could make in scraping off a little bit of hay
October 25, 1971

every day from his horse that he did not look at the horse, and as a result ended up penny wise and pound foolish: he lost the horse at the end of the process. I do not consider the farmer was a particularly wise person, and I think this government is exceedingly unwise to do what it is doing with the low-income people of this country.
Evidently this government does not worry if someone says it is heartless and does not care. What worries the government is if it is told it is inefficient and not up on modern ways of technology and monetary success. I suggest that by going ahead and scraping and scraping away the livelihood of the low-income people who earn the wages and do the work in this country, the government is following a very foolish procedure indeed. Do not forget: the difference between the farmer's horse and the people on low income in this country is that the low wage earners are learning very slowly but surely that they are simply being robbed a little more, a little more and a little more.
I know people in my riding, and I am sure hon. members opposite know people in their constituencies, who are working for small wages, who are very self-respecting, who are very independent in their jobs, whose problems are increasing just as steadily as the burdens the government is placing on them in the way of increased taxation, who have children to feed and clothe and who must pay high rents. Remember, when the cost of food, clothing and rent steadily increases over a period, a few points here and a few points there, and the cost of living is going up steadily in this country, the low wage earners know this very well and feel it.
These people must have food and clothing. They have to pay as much for their bread, meat and other food items as do people like ourselves who took occasion to raise our own income because it was felt it was no longer adequate to buy food and clothing and to pay for the shelter and other things which Members of Parliament need. People who are earning low salaries and incomes have to pay the same amount for groceries as the rest of us. They have no way to prevent the landlord from continually raising the rent bit by bit by bit.
These are the people who see the opportunities they thought they had to send their young folk to school and college whittled away because the cost of living has not left them enough to carry on the education of their children. This is what is happening across the country. The people are beginning slowly, but very surely, to understand what is happening. I think this government received a nasty shock over the last few weeks when it discovered that the farmers in western Canada were not going to accept something they did not want and that the government could not tell them in fancy language that it knew far better what the farmers and farm organizations wanted. The people on the Prairies said they did not want it and were not going to take it. They were not going to be told it was better for them than what they wanted.
I warn the government that across the country there are thousands and thousands of families who know what they want and they are gradually reaching the point where they Will completely reject this government. What for? For complete unfairness and discrimination. They know very well that the government has allowed the higher wage and salary earners and large corporations in this country to get away with far less than their share of the
Income Tax Act
tax burden, and that a far greater share has been loaded on the low wage earner and people with small incomes.
That gentleman of the cloth over there can smile all he likes. If he were following the teaching he was raised on he would know it is very bad to grind the faces of the poor and get after the poor widows, fatherless children, and so on. But since he has been on that side of the House he has forgotten all the teachings he had in his early youth.
I have just returned from my riding where I saw once again how hard people are trying to have faith in this Parliament and how much they are hoping it will give them an opportunity to make their own way in decency. I become angry because it seems so hopeless to get Members of Parliament on the other side to realize what they are doing to the wage earners in this country. Heaven alone knowws why they are doing it, because they have had enough warnings to realize that they cannot get away with it. There is no use their using the old excuse that they have to put these imposts on-

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I will speak to what is relevant whether or not these people think it is. My colleague, the hon. member for Broadview, has demol-
